I want to replace that with the true version, because the true version is simpler and it predicts the behavior of let and const correctly, which the move to the top story can't do. So today we correct the story, and we'll model it properly in scope.js.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Here is the truth. Before a scope's code runs, the engine does a pass through the scope and creates bindings for every declaration in it. Nothing moves in the source. The bindings just exist from the start of the scope, and what differs is how they are initialized. A var declaration is created and immediately initialized to undefined. A function declaration is created and initialized to the whole function. A let or const declaration is created but left uninitialized. Three different starting states, and that's all hoisting is.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Let's see what that means. Write console.log of a, then var a equals five. It prints undefined, because the binding existed and was undefined. Now write console.log of b, then let b equals five. You get a ReferenceError, cannot access b before initialization. The binding exists, the engine knows about it, which is why it doesn't say b is not defined, but it's in a state called the temporal dead zone, from the start of the scope until the line with the declaration runs. Temporal, because it's about time, not about position in the text.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Now let's put this into mini-runtime. In scope.js I'll add a method called hoist that takes a list of declarations, each with a name and a kind. For var, it calls declare with undefined. For function, it declares with the function value. For let and const, it stores a special symbol called UNINITIALIZED. Then in lookup, if the value we find is that symbol, we throw a ReferenceError saying cannot access the name before initialization. And we add an initialize method that replaces the symbol when the declaration line executes. Run the example from before and our model behaves exactly like Node.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: So what should you do in practice with all this? Prefer const by default, and let when you need to reassign, and avoid var. That way you never depend on the undefined initial state, and any early use fails loudly with a clear ReferenceError rather than silently giving you undefined. And declare things before using them, even for functions, even though function declarations would work. The model is clear now, so the code you write should not rely on its odd corners.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
text: Two gotchas to finish. First, function expressions are not hoisted like declarations. If you write var greet equals a function, then greet is undefined until that line, and calling it early throws a TypeError, greet is not a function. Second, the typeof operator used to be safe on undeclared names, but it throws inside the temporal dead zone. That surprised a lot of people when let arrived. Both of these follow from the model. Next lecture, we'll look at what happens when a function leaves its scope and still needs it. That's closures.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: This is the lecture where scope pays off. A closure is a function together with the scope it was created in. That's the entire definition. People make it sound mystical, but with the Scope class we built it is almost trivial, and today we'll see why. We'll make functions in mini-runtime carry a reference to their defining scope, and then we'll watch a counter survive after the function that made it has returned. Let's go through it slowly, since everything we did so far leads here.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: Start with the classic example in real JavaScript. A function makeCounter declares let count equals zero and returns a function that increments count and returns it. Call makeCounter, store the result as next, and call next three times. You get one, two, three. Here's the puzzle. makeCounter has returned. Its execution context was popped off the call stack. So where is count living? If variables lived on the stack, it would be gone. It isn't gone, because the scope object isn't stored on the stack. It's an ordinary object on the heap, and the returned function holds a reference to it.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: So in our model we add one thing. When a function is created, we record the current scope on it. In runtime.js I'll write createFunction, taking a name, params, a body, and the current scope, and returning an object `{ name, params, body, closure: scope }`. Then in callFunction, instead of making a new scope whose parent is the caller's scope, we make one whose parent is fn dot closure. That single line is the difference between lexical and dynamic scope, and it's the entire closure mechanism.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: Let's run it. Build makeCounter in our model, call it, keep the returned function, call it three times, and print. We get one, two, three. Then create a second counter and notice it starts from one again, because each call to makeCounter created a fresh Scope with its own count. Two closures, two scope objects, no sharing. This is also why closures are used for private state. Nobody outside can reach count, because the only access is through the function that holds the scope.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: To close, let's recap what we built. Functions now carry a closure field, calls create a scope whose parent is that field, and scopes live on the heap so they outlive stack frames. Our callstack.js still pushes and pops frames, but the frame's env is now a Scope whose chain can reach back to where the function was defined. Notice how little code that took. Closures aren't a feature that was added to the language, they're what you get automatically from lexical scope plus first-class functions.

lecture_title: 2.3 - Closures: Functions That Remember Their Scope
text: Now the famous loop bug. A for loop with var i, pushing functions into an array that log i, then calling them after the loop prints the final value every time, because all the functions share the one function-level scope and its single i. Change var to let, and each iteration gets its own block scope, so each function sees its own i. In our model that's just creating a new Scope per iteration. One last warning, closures keep the whole scope alive, which can hold large objects in memory, so release references you don't need. Next chapter we deal with this, the value of this.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Now we get to the most argued-about keyword in JavaScript, this. And the good news is that it follows exactly four rules, and once you know them you can predict this by reading the call site. Not the function definition, the call site, which is the single most important thing to take from today. So we'll learn the four rules, then add them to mini-runtime so callFunction can compute a value of this for every call.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Rule one, default binding. If you call a plain function, like greet with parentheses and nothing in front, then this is the global object, or undefined in strict mode. Modules and classes are always strict, so in most modern code you get undefined. That's why pulling a method off an object and calling it alone loses its this. Rule two, implicit binding. If you call it as obj dot method, then this is the object in front of the dot. Only the last object counts, so a dot b dot method gives this equal to b.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Rule three, explicit binding. Using call, apply or bind lets you choose this directly. Call and apply invoke the function immediately, with arguments listed or in an array. Bind returns a new function with this permanently fixed. Rule four, new binding. If you call a function with the new keyword, a fresh object is created and this points to it. We'll implement that one in the next lecture. The priority order, if rules conflict, is new first, then explicit, then implicit, then default. Bind beats a dot call, for example.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Arrow functions are the exception, and they're not a fifth rule. An arrow function has no this of its own. It looks up this the same way it looks up any variable, through the scope chain, so it takes the this of the scope where it was written. That's lexical, like everything else we built. It also means call, apply and bind can't change an arrow's this. This is why arrows are great for callbacks inside methods, and a bad idea for object methods that need their own object.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: A quick exercise before we leave this. Take an object with a name property and a method that logs this dot name. Call it directly and it works. Assign the method to a variable and call that, and you get undefined or an error. Pass it to setTimeout, same problem. Now fix it three ways, with bind, with an arrow wrapper, and with a class field arrow function. For each fix, say which rule is now in play. If you can do that, you've got this.

lecture_title: 3.1 - How this Gets Bound: The Four Rules
text: Let's code it. In runtime.js, callFunction now takes a thisArg parameter. I'll write a helper resolveThis that takes the call description. If the call has isNew, create an object. If it has an explicit receiver from call or bind, use that. If it has an object before the dot, use it. Otherwise return undefined, because our runtime is strict. Store the result in the new scope under the name this. For arrows, skip storing it, so lookup walks outward. Test with a detached method, and you'll see undefined. Next, constructors and what new really does.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: In the last lecture we listed four binding rules and left the last one, new, for today. The new keyword looks like magic, but it's a short recipe, four steps, and once you can write those steps in code you will never be confused by constructors again. We'll implement a function called construct in runtime.js, and along the way we'll meet the first real piece of prototype machinery, which prepares us for chapter four. So let's build it.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: Here is the setup in plain JavaScript. A constructor function is just a normal function that we call with new, by convention with a capital letter. function Dog taking a name, setting this dot name equals name. Then new Dog, with the string Rex, gives us an object with a name property. Nothing in the function created that object. We never wrote return. So who did? The new operator did, and the steps are the same every time. Take a moment to see that this is a pattern you've used many times.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: The four steps. One, create a brand new empty object. Two, set that object's internal prototype to the constructor's prototype property, which is where the object will look for things it doesn't have. Three, call the constructor with this bound to the new object, passing along the arguments. Four, if the constructor returned an object, use that as the result, otherwise use the new object from step one. Step four is a rarely used detail, but it's why returning a primitive from a constructor is simply ignored.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: Now in code. In runtime.js I'll write construct, taking a function and an args array. First, `const obj = Object.create(fn.prototype)`, which does steps one and two in one go. Next we call the function through callFunction with the thisArg set to obj. Store that in result. Then `return (typeof result === 'object' && result !== null) || typeof result === 'function' ? result : obj`. That's all of new. Try it with Dog, and check that Object.getPrototypeOf of the result is Dog dot prototype. It is.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: A common mistake is forgetting new. If you call Dog without it, the default binding rule applies, so this is undefined in strict code and the assignment throws, or it quietly sets a property on the global object in sloppy mode. That's why ES6 classes throw an error if called without new, and why older code had a check at the top, if this is not an instance of Dog, return new Dog. Both are guarding against the same thing. You now understand why that guard existed.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
text: And this tells us where methods should go. If I write this dot bark equals a function inside Dog, every instance gets its own copy of that function, and a thousand dogs means a thousand functions. If I instead write Dog dot prototype dot bark, there is one function, and every dog finds it through the link set in step two. That link, and how lookup follows it, is the topic of the whole next chapter. Take a break, then we go into prototype inheritance, and we'll write proto.js.

Welcome to chapter four. We finished the last chapter with new setting up a link between an object and its constructor's prototype. Today we find out what that link is for, and we write proto.js, the prototype lookup of mini-runtime. This is the topic that trips up more developers than any other in the language, so I'll go slowly. And I'll start with a definition that I want you to hear carefully, because everything else this chapter hangs off it.

Prototype inheritance is the mechanism by which objects in JavaScript inherit properties and methods from other objects. Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object called its prototype, accessible as __proto__. When you access a property on an object and JavaScript cannot find it directly on that object, it walks up the prototype chain automatically until it either finds the property or reaches null at the top of the chain. This prototype lookup is invisible to you but happens on every single property access.

Let's see this live. Open a Node REPL and type `const animal = { eats: true }`, then `const dog = Object.create(animal)`. Now `dog.eats` gives true, even though dog has no own property called eats. Check with `dog.hasOwnProperty('eats')`, which is false. And `Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal` is true. Next set `dog.barks = true`. That goes on dog itself, not on animal, because assignment always writes to the object you are assigning on. Reading walks the chain, writing doesn't. Keep that asymmetry in mind, it explains a lot of surprising bugs.

Think of prototype inheritance as a delegation chain, not a copy. If object A has object B as its prototype, and you look for a method on A that does not exist there, JavaScript automatically delegates the lookup to B. This chain continues all the way up to Object.prototype which is the root. The key insight is that objects do not copy properties from their prototype. They delegate lookups to it at runtime. This delegation model is what makes prototype inheritance both powerful and memory-efficient. All instances share one copy of inherited methods rather than each having their own copy.

Now let's model it in proto.js. I'll write a function getProperty taking an object and a key. Inside, a loop with `let current = obj`, and while current is not null, if current has its own key, return its value, otherwise set current to Object.getPrototypeOf of current. After the loop, return undefined. That's the whole lookup, about six lines. Let me also write setProperty, which just does `obj[key] = value`, because writes ignore the chain, with one exception, setters, which we'll skip. Test it with the animal and dog we made, and a three-level chain, and watch it climb.

Let me show where all those built-in methods come from. Create an empty object and call `toString` on it. You never defined that. It's found on Object.prototype, which sits at the top, and its own prototype is null. An array goes one level deeper, the array's prototype is Array.prototype, which holds map and filter, and whose prototype is Object.prototype. That's why arrays also have hasOwnProperty. And since the chain is live, if you add a method to a prototype, every existing object sees it immediately. Powerful, and also why modifying built-in prototypes is considered dangerous.

When you use the class syntax in modern JavaScript it is still prototype-based inheritance under the hood. The class keyword is purely syntactic sugar. When you write class Dog extends Animal, JavaScript sets up the prototype chain so that Dog.prototype has Animal.prototype as its prototype. The instanceof operator also relies on this chain to check if an object was derived from a particular constructor function. Understanding the prototype chain helps you debug unexpected behavior when properties seem to appear from nowhere or when you accidentally shadow a prototype method.

One more debugging tip before we move on. When a property shows up from nowhere, use a loop that walks the chain and prints each object that has that key as an own property. We can build that straight from getProperty, we'll call it findOwner, returning the object where the property was found. And when you see shadowing, where an own property hides one further up, findOwner will show you. Next time we dig into classes, and see that they are exactly what we've just built with nicer syntax.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Last lecture we built a prototype lookup. Now let's look at the thing most of you actually write, the class keyword. The claim today is that a class adds no new object model. It is a cleaner way of writing the constructor function and prototype dance we've already done. To prove it, we'll take a class and desugar it by hand, and then add class support to mini-runtime's proto.js in about twenty lines. Let's go step by step and see for ourselves.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Start with a class. `class Animal` with a constructor taking name and setting this dot name, and a method speak that logs the name. Check what you get. `typeof Animal` is function. `Animal.prototype.speak` is the method you wrote. `Animal.prototype.constructor === Animal` is true. So the class is a function, and the methods live on its prototype object, exactly like in the constructor-function version. A few differences exist, class bodies are strict, the methods aren't enumerable, and calling a class without new throws. But the structure is identical.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Now inheritance. `class Dog extends Animal`, with a constructor that calls super of name, then sets this dot tricks. What does extends actually do? Two links. One, `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype)` equals Animal.prototype, so instances of Dog find speak through the chain. Two, `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog)` equals Animal, so static methods are inherited too, which people often forget. A call to super is basically calling the parent constructor so that it initializes this. In a derived class you can't touch this before super returns, since the object is created by the base class.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Let's write the desugared version by hand in proto.js. A function defineClass takes a name, an optional parent, a constructor function and a methods object. It creates the function, then sets `fn.prototype = Object.create(parent ? parent.prototype : Object.prototype)`. Then it sets `fn.prototype.constructor = fn`, and copies each method onto fn.prototype. If there is a parent, it calls `Object.setPrototypeOf(fn, parent)` for statics. Return fn. Now define Animal and Dog with it, create a dog, call speak, and you'll see it works just like the real syntax.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Let me add a caution about how people use classes in JavaScript, because the sugar can hide costs. Inheritance hierarchies more than two levels deep make the chain longer, and every miss walks further. They also couple code tightly, a change in a base class ripples into everything below it. Many teams prefer composition, small objects combined together, or functions that return objects. Both styles are fine, but now that you know classes are just prototypes, you can choose with open eyes, instead of copying an object-oriented habit from another language, okay?

lecture_title: 4.2 - Classes Are Sugar Over the Prototype Chain
text: Here's a payoff for the model. Private fields with the hash prefix are different, they are not on the chain, they're stored in a hidden per-object slot, so they cannot be accessed by lookup at all. That's by design. Also, methods defined as arrow function class fields are own properties on each instance, not shared, so they cost memory per object, though they bind this lexically. Both of these become obvious once you ask, is it on the prototype or on the instance? In the next lecture we write the two operators that depend on this chain.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Today's lecture is pure building. We've talked about the prototype chain for two lectures, and the best test of whether you really understand a mechanism is to write it yourself. So we will implement Object.create and instanceof from scratch in proto.js, without using the built-in versions. Along the way we'll use only two primitives that the language gives us, getPrototypeOf and setPrototypeOf, plus a function's prototype property. These are two of the most asked-about topics in interviews, and after today you will be able to answer with code, not just words.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Let's begin with create. Object.create takes a prototype and returns a new empty object whose prototype is that value. Our version, myCreate, takes proto. First a guard, if proto is not an object and not null, throw a TypeError. Then there are two ways to build it. The modern way is `const obj = {}; Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto); return obj;`. The old way, which was the polyfill for years, creates a throwaway constructor `function F() {}`, sets `F.prototype = proto`, and returns `new F()`. Both give the same result, and the second one shows that new is doing the link for us.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Test it. `const a = { x: 1 }; const b = myCreate(a);` Then `b.x` is one, and `Object.getPrototypeOf(b) === a` is true. Also try myCreate with null, and you get an object with no prototype at all, so `b.toString` is undefined. People use that to build pure dictionaries, where keys like constructor or hasOwnProperty can't collide with inherited names. One caveat is that setPrototypeOf on an existing object can slow V8 down, because it changes the object's shape after the fact. Remember that, we'll see why in chapter five.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Now instanceof. The expression `obj instanceof Ctor` asks, does Ctor.prototype appear anywhere in obj's prototype chain? So our myInstanceOf takes obj and Ctor. If obj is not an object, return false. Take `const target = Ctor.prototype`, then `let current = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`, and loop. If current is null, return false. If current is strictly equal to target, return true. Otherwise move up. That's it. The real operator also checks for a Symbol dot hasInstance method first, which lets a class customize the test, but the chain walk is the core.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Here's a bonus that connects to something you'll see in real codebases. Object.create takes an optional second argument, a map of property descriptors, so you can define properties that are not writable or not enumerable at creation time. We won't implement descriptors, but it's worth knowing they exist, since Object.defineProperty is what class syntax uses under the hood for its non-enumerable methods. If you want an extra challenge, extend myCreate to accept a descriptor map and apply each entry with defineProperty.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Writing Object.create and instanceof by Hand
text: Let's test with the classes from the last lecture. A dog is an instance of Dog, of Animal and of Object, and not of Array. Now the sneaky case. Create dog, then reassign `Dog.prototype = {}`. Now `dog instanceof Dog` is false, because the chain no longer contains the new prototype object. This is a classic reason instanceof lies across realms too, like between iframes, where each frame has its own Array. That's why Array.isArray exists. You now own two core pieces of the language. Next chapter, we leave the language and look at the engine under it.

We now step under the language, into V8, the engine that runs inside Chrome and Node. So far we've modeled how JavaScript behaves. In this chapter we ask how it can be fast, because the model we built, walking chains and looking up names in maps, sounds slow. And it would be, if the engine really did that every time. Let's see how it avoids it, starting with the single most important idea in the engine's object representation.

V8, the JavaScript engine inside Node.js and Chrome, uses hidden classes to optimize property access on objects. When you create an object and add properties to it, V8 creates an internal hidden class that describes the shape of that object. Hidden classes are similar to structs in C. Every time you add a new property to an object V8 creates a new hidden class and transitions the object to it. This is how V8 avoids the overhead of a hash table lookup on every property access and can instead use fast fixed-offset memory access.

Let me draw this out. Imagine `const p = {}`. V8 gives it an initial hidden class, call it C0, describing an empty shape. Then `p.x = 1` creates a new hidden class C1, which says there is a property x at offset zero, and records the transition from C0 to C1 on the key x. Then `p.y = 2` makes C2, with x at offset zero and y at offset one, via a transition from C1. The object itself now stores just the values in order, and a pointer to its current hidden class. The shape lives in one place, shared by everyone with that shape.

The critical thing to understand about V8 hidden classes is that two objects that look identical to you can end up with completely different hidden classes if you add properties in a different order. If you create object A and add x then y, and create object B and add y then x, V8 sees them as different shapes and cannot optimize them the same way. This also means dynamically adding properties after object construction, especially in conditionals or loops, causes hidden class transitions that hurt performance significantly in hot code paths.

You can actually see this. In Node, run a script with the flag `--allow-natives-syntax` and call `%HaveSameMap(a, b)`, which returns true if two objects share a hidden class. Create `a = { x: 1, y: 2 }` and `b = { x: 3, y: 4 }`, same literal, and it's true. Now create `c = { y: 4, x: 3 }` and the result is false against a. Same keys, same values, different order, different shape. It's the cleanest demonstration I know. And in our mini-runtime we'll add a small shapes.js that records transitions, so you can print the shape chain yourself.

Let me do that now. In shapes.js, a class Shape with an id, a Map called transitions, and a Map called offsets. A function addProperty takes a shape and a key. If the shape already has a transition for the key, return it, otherwise create a new Shape that copies offsets and adds the key at the next offset, store it in transitions, and return it. Create a root shape, add x, add y, and again from the root add y, add x. Print ids, and you'll see two separate branches, which is exactly the situation the engine finds itself in.

To write V8-friendly code, always initialize all object properties in the constructor in the same order every time. Never add new properties to an object after construction if you can avoid it. Avoid delete operator on properties as it forces V8 to switch to a slower dictionary mode. Prefer setting a property to null instead of deleting it. When you follow these patterns V8 can share hidden classes across all instances of the same constructor, leading to significant speedups through inline caching and JIT compilation.

There's one practical thing I want to leave you with. Don't over-apply this. Hidden classes matter in hot code, meaning loops and functions called thousands of times, with many objects of the same kind, like particles or rows. In code that runs once, shape consistency changes nothing you can measure. Profile first. Next lecture, we find out what V8 does with these shapes at each property access, which is inline caching, and why code that sees only one shape is the fastest of all.

In the last lecture we learned that V8 gives every object a hidden class. But a shape by itself doesn't make anything fast. It's what V8 does with that shape at each property access site that matters. Today we study inline caches, and the terms monomorphic, polymorphic and megamorphic, which you'll see in performance articles and profiling tools. And then we'll simulate an inline cache in mini-runtime so you can watch it hit and miss.

Consider a function `function getX(p) { return p.x }`. The first time it runs, V8 doesn't know where x lives in p, so it does the slow generic lookup. But then it remembers. At that exact spot in the code, it stores a small cache, saying, if the object's hidden class is C1, then x is at offset zero. That's an inline cache. The next call checks one thing, is this object's hidden class C1, and if so, reads memory at offset zero directly. One comparison and one load, no lookup, no prototype walk.

Now the states. If the site has only ever seen one hidden class, it's monomorphic, the fastest state. If it has seen two to four different classes, it's polymorphic, and the cache holds a short list that it checks one by one, still decent. If it sees more than that, it becomes megamorphic and falls back to a shared global lookup table, and that is significantly slower. And the optimizing compiler, TurboFan, can inline and optimize the monomorphic sites best, because it can bake in the assumption about the shape.

Let's simulate this in mini-runtime. In shapes.js I'll add makeSite, which returns a function with a cache array. When called with an object, it reads the object's shape. If the shape is in the cache, it increments hits and returns the value from the stored offset. Otherwise it does the slow lookup, increments misses, pushes the shape into the cache, and if the cache grows beyond four entries, it sets a flag called megamorphic and stops caching. Feed it fifty objects of one shape and print the stats, forty-nine hits and one miss.

Let me give you some honest guidance on what to do with this. Don't contort your code to chase monomorphism everywhere. Do three simple things. Create objects of the same kind with the same constructor or factory, so they share a shape. Initialize all fields up front, even if the value is null for now. And avoid passing wildly different object kinds through a hot function, split it when it makes sense. Beyond that, measure with a profiler, because engine details change from version to version, and the principles last longer than the specifics.

Now feed it objects built with different key orders, five different shapes, and watch it go megamorphic and the miss counter climb. This is why a function that handles very different object kinds, like a general utility called with everything in your app, is slower than several specialized ones. It's also why TypeScript style discipline, consistent object shapes, helps performance as a side effect. We'll use this when we trace a bug through the layers at the end of the course. Right now though, we move to the other half of the story, the event loop.

Welcome to chapter six, the one that explains why JavaScript can wait for a network request without freezing. So far everything we've modeled has been synchronous, one call after another, on one stack. But real programs have timers, clicks and fetches. To handle them, the runtime wraps the engine in a loop, and today we'll understand that loop precisely, including the part with promises that catches out even experienced people. Let's start with the definition, and then we'll test it.

JavaScript runs on a single thread, so it can only do one thing at a time. The event loop is the mechanism that lets it stay responsive despite that. There is a call stack where function calls are pushed and popped, and a task queue (the macrotask queue) where callbacks from things like setTimeout, I/O, and DOM events wait. The event loop has one simple rule: when the call stack is empty, take the next task from the queue and run it to completion. 'Run to completion' is key — a task is never interrupted halfway, which is why long synchronous work freezes the page.

Let's check it with a classic puzzle. Write console.log one, then setTimeout with a callback logging two and a delay of zero, then console.log three. The output is one, three, two. Why? The main script is itself a task. It runs to completion, logging one and three, and the timer callback sits in the macrotask queue until the stack is empty. Note that a delay of zero doesn't mean now, it means as soon as possible after the current task, and browsers and Node also enforce a small minimum.

Promises do not use the macrotask queue. They use a separate, higher-priority microtask queue. After every single task finishes and before the event loop picks up the next macrotask, it completely drains the microtask queue. This is why a resolved Promise's .then callback always runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0) scheduled at the same time — microtasks jump the line. The practical consequence: if you schedule microtasks that themselves schedule more microtasks, you can starve the macrotask queue and block rendering. await is just syntax over .then, so the code after an await also runs as a microtask.

Now the real puzzle. Script logs start, then setTimeout logging timeout, then `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'))`, then logs end. The output is start, end, promise, timeout. Walk through it. The script task logs start and end. Its callbacks are registered, the timer in the macrotask queue and the promise reaction in the microtask queue. When the script task finishes, the microtask queue is drained, so promise prints. Only then does the loop take the timer task. Practice drawing the two queues on paper for a few programs, until it's automatic.

Let me show the starvation problem I mentioned. Write a function `function loop() { Promise.resolve().then(loop) }` and call it. The page, or in Node the whole process, never gets to timers or I/O, because the microtask queue never becomes empty. It's an infinite loop that doesn't look like one, since each step is asynchronous. Compare this with `setTimeout(loop, 0)`, which lets other tasks and rendering interleave. Node adds one more detail, process.nextTick has its own queue that runs even before promise microtasks. We'll keep that outside our model but know it exists.

So, to summarize what we need to build. A call stack, which we have. A macrotask queue, a microtask queue, and a loop that runs one task, then drains microtasks, then repeats. In the browser there's also a rendering step between tasks, which is why long tasks cause janky pages. Next lecture we code all of that in eventloop.js, and then we'll run the puzzles from today through our own simulator and see the same output. If you want to prepare, think about what data structure each queue should be.

Today we write eventloop.js. In the last lecture we described the machine in words, two queues and a loop. Now we make it real, and by the end you'll run the setTimeout and promise puzzles through your own simulator and get exactly the output Node gives. I think this is the most satisfying lecture in the course, because it's short code that explains a huge amount of real-world behavior. So open your editor, create eventloop.js, and follow along with me.

Let's set up the pieces. In eventloop.js I'll create a class EventLoop with three fields. `macrotasks`, an array used as a queue, `microtasks`, another array, and `timers`, a list of objects with a callback and a due time, plus a `now` field that is our fake clock. Using a fake clock is a deliberate choice, because it makes the simulator deterministic, and we can test it without waiting. Then methods. `setTimeout(fn, delay)` pushes `{ fn, due: this.now + delay }` into timers, and `queueMicrotask(fn)` pushes fn into microtasks.

Now the heart, the method run. It takes the main script as a function. First, wrap the script as the first macrotask by pushing it to macrotasks. Then a loop. While there is any work, meaning macrotasks, timers or microtasks left, do the following. If the macrotask queue is empty, advance now to the earliest due timer and move every timer that is due into macrotasks, sorted by due time and insertion order. Then shift one macrotask and run it to completion. Then call drainMicrotasks, and repeat. That's one turn of the loop.

The drain is a small piece. `drainMicrotasks()` does `while (this.microtasks.length) { const fn = this.microtasks.shift(); fn(); }`. Notice that it keeps going even when fn pushes new microtasks, because the length is checked each time. That single detail reproduces the starvation behavior we discussed. I'll also add a guard counter in our simulator that throws after a million microtasks, so our own infinite-microtask test doesn't hang the terminal. A real engine has no such guard, which is exactly why it hangs.

Let's extend the simulator one step further, to see how a promise fits in. I'll write a tiny class MyPromise in eventloop.js with a state, a value and a list of callbacks. Its then method, if the promise is already settled, calls loop dot queueMicrotask with the callback, otherwise it stores the callback to be queued on resolve. Resolve sets the state and queues every stored callback as a microtask. That's the whole trick. Native promises are more careful about thenables and error handling, but the scheduling idea is exactly this.

Let's run the puzzle. Write a script function that logs start, calls loop dot setTimeout with a callback logging timeout and a delay of zero, calls loop dot queueMicrotask with one logging promise, and logs end. Pass it to loop dot run. Output, start, end, promise, timeout. Now add a second timer with a smaller delay and see it fire first, and a microtask scheduled inside a timer callback and see it run right after that callback, before the next timer. Same as the real thing. Next time we use this machine to understand async and await, which is simply a friendlier way to write promise chains.

In this lecture we finish chapter six by putting a friendly face on the machine. Async and await look like a different feature, almost like threads, but they're built from promises, and promises are built on the microtask queue we just simulated. The takeaway statement, and I want you to say it with me, is that await is just then underneath. We'll prove it by rewriting async functions as then chains and by predicting some tricky output order.

Start with the basics. An async function always returns a promise. If it returns a value, the promise resolves with it, and if it throws, the promise rejects. Inside, the await keyword pauses that function, not the thread. It takes a promise, or wraps a plain value in a resolved promise, and arranges for the rest of the function to run as a microtask continuation when the promise settles. Meanwhile the caller carries on. That's why code after calling an async function runs before the code after the await inside it.

Here's a puzzle. `async function f() { console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b'); }`, then call f, then log c. The output is a, c, b. Step by step. Calling f runs synchronously up to the first await, so a prints. The await schedules the continuation as a microtask and returns control to the caller, which prints c. Then the stack is empty, the microtask runs, and b prints. The equivalent without async is `console.log('a'); Promise.resolve(null).then(() => console.log('b'))`. Same order, same mechanism.

Let's make it more interesting by mixing with a timer. Add a setTimeout logging t before the call to f. Now the output is a, c, b, t. The microtask continuation, b, always beats the timer. And if f awaits a promise that resolves from a timer, say a promise that resolves inside setTimeout with a delay of fifty, then the continuation waits for that timer task, and after the timer callback finishes its microtasks drain, and b prints. In our simulator you can verify all this by writing the promise logic ourselves as a tiny class with then, using queueMicrotask, in about twenty lines.

Let me summarize with a translation rule you can use whenever you are confused. Take an async function, and split its body at each await. Everything before the first await runs synchronously when called. Each remaining piece becomes a function passed to then on the awaited promise, and the function's returned promise resolves with whatever the last piece returns. A try and catch around an await becomes a catch on the chain. If you can do that translation in your head, you can predict any ordering question an interviewer or a bug throws at you.

Two practical warnings. First, await inside a loop makes iterations sequential. If the operations are independent, collect the promises and use Promise.all, so they run concurrently. Second, an error thrown after an await is a rejected promise, so wrap the awaited code in try and catch, or the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes modern Node by default. Also, forgetting to await a promise is silent, the code after just keeps going. Now we have all the layers, stack, scope, prototypes, shapes and loop. In the final chapter, we'll use them together.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: This is the capstone. For six chapters we built pieces of mini-runtime, and in this lecture I want you to see them work together on a realistic bug. I'll show you a small program that misbehaves in a confusing way, and we'll debug it by asking at each layer what the model says should happen. The point isn't the bug itself, it's the method, going down through the layers until the surprise disappears. So let's get started.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Here's the program. A small task tracker, with a class Task, created with a title and a list of tags. A function loadTasks that runs a loop for each id, and calls fetchTask with a delay, using setTimeout in the callback to push results into an array called results. After the loop, the code logs results dot length and expects three, but prints zero. Also, a second symptom, when tasks finally appear, every one has the same id. Two bugs, one program, and they sit in different layers.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Take the first symptom, results dot length is zero. Which layer? The event loop. The callbacks passed to setTimeout are macrotasks, they run only after the current script task finishes and the stack is empty. The log line runs in the current task, so results is still empty. It's not a timing mystery, it's the run-to-completion rule. We confirm by running the program through our EventLoop simulator, and the log happens before any timer callback. The fix is to return a promise, await all the work, and only then log.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Second symptom, every task has the same id. Which layer? Scope and closures. The loop uses var i, and the setTimeout callback closes over i. By the time any callback runs, the loop has finished and i is three, and all callbacks share the single function-level scope. In our Scope model, there's one binding for i. Switch to let, each iteration gets its own block scope with its own i, and each closure captures its own. We can demonstrate this in runtime.js by creating a new Scope per iteration.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Let me put the fixed version together so you can compare. The Task constructor now sets title, id and tags in one fixed order, with tags defaulting to an empty array. The loadTasks function is async, uses a for of loop with let, and awaits Promise.all over the fetches, then logs the length, three. Run it and the numbers are right, the ids are distinct, and a profile shows a single shape for Task. The skill here wasn't memorizing fixes, it was asking, which layer is responsible, and answering from the model.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Tracing One Bug Through Every Layer
text: Now a third, quieter issue that shows up in profiling. Tasks created in loadTasks sometimes have a tags property and sometimes not, depending on the data, and the code adds tags afterward when present. Which layer? Hidden classes. Objects of the same class end up with two shapes, so a hot function reading task dot tags sees two shapes, polymorphic, and if more variations appear, megamorphic. The fix is to always initialize tags in the constructor, to an empty array if there are none. Three symptoms, three layers, and no magic involved.

Well, we made it to the end. Let me start by saying congratulations, because you did something most JavaScript developers never do. You looked under the hood, and not just looked, you rebuilt it. Let me recap what mini-runtime contains now. A callstack.js with frames and stack traces. A scope.js with the scope chain, hoisting and closures. A proto.js with prototype lookup, classes, and hand-written create and instanceof. A shapes.js with hidden class transitions and inline caches. And an eventloop.js with macrotasks, microtasks and a fake clock.

Let me also summarize the mental models, because those are the real product. Execution is a stack of contexts. Names are resolved by walking a chain of scopes determined by where code is written. The value of this is determined by how a function is called, except for arrows. Objects delegate to their prototypes at runtime, and classes are sugar over that. The engine assigns shapes, and rewards consistency. And everything asynchronous goes through two queues, with microtasks always drained between tasks. If you can explain each of those without notes, you've learned the course.

Here's what I'd suggest you do next. First, extend mini-runtime on your own. Add getters and setters to proto.js, so lookups invoke accessor functions. Add generators or async iteration to the event loop. Add a simple garbage collector that marks scopes reachable from the stack and sweeps the rest, which makes closures and memory leaks very concrete. Each of these is a weekend project, and each teaches you something that reading never will. Don't try to make it complete, it's a teaching model, and the gaps are where you learn.

Second, go and read primary sources. The ECMAScript specification is more readable than people think, especially the sections on function calls and the abstract operations like OrdinaryGet, which is literally our prototype lookup. The V8 blog has excellent posts on hidden classes, Ignition and TurboFan, and the Node.js docs on the event loop describe the phases in detail. When you read them now, you'll recognize every concept, and the vocabulary won't be a barrier anymore. Use Chrome devtools and node dash dash inspect to look at real scope chains and profiles as well.

Let me end with one honest note on learning. You will forget details, and that's fine. What stays is the shape of the model, and your ability to rebuild a piece of it when you need it. When you meet a new framework, ask what it does with scope, with this, with objects, and with the event loop, because every framework is a set of choices about those same five things. Thank you again, and keep building. Share your mini-runtime extensions with other learners, teaching it back is the best way to lock it in.

Third, use this in your daily work. The next time you see a confusing bug, ask which layer it lives in. Stack, scope, this, prototype, shape or queue. That habit alone will make you faster at debugging than most of your peers. And if you want to go deeper, we have courses on browser APIs and on React performance, which apply exactly these ideas. Thank you for building this with me. Go and break something in mini-runtime on purpose and fix it. I'll see you in the next course.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Welcome to Web APIs and Real-Time. In this course we're going to answer a question that sounds simple and turns out to have a lot of layers: how does a server tell a browser that something just happened? Think about a live cricket or football scoreboard. A goal goes in, and within a second every person watching sees the number change without touching refresh. By the end of this course you'll know exactly how that works, and more importantly, you'll know what each approach costs you, so you can choose on purpose instead of copying whatever a tutorial used.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Here's the project. We're going to build a live match scoreboard. There's a small Node server, built with Express, that holds a single object called `matchState`. It has the home team, the away team, the two scores, and the match clock. There's also a little simulator that changes that state every few seconds, so goals and fouls keep happening while we work. And there's a plain HTML page, `scoreboard.html`, with a script called `scoreboard.js` that needs to keep the numbers on screen current.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: The interesting part is that we will deliver those updates to the browser four different ways. First, short polling, where the page just asks again and again. Second, long-polling, where the server holds the question open until it has an answer. Third, Server-Sent Events, which is a one-way stream over normal HTTP. And fourth, WebSockets, a full-duplex connection that starts life as an HTTP request and then switches protocols. Same scoreboard, same data, four transports. That's the best way I know to feel the differences.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: The course has five parts. We start with HTTP and polling, so you understand why plain request and response can't push anything. Then we cross the boundary into WebSockets by studying the Upgrade handshake and what frames look like on the wire. After that we compare the transports properly, with real measurements of bytes, latency and open connections. Then we deal with the part most tutorials skip, which is resilience: reconnecting with backoff, heartbeats, and backpressure. We finish by shipping the scoreboard with one transport per feature.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: What do you need coming in? Basic JavaScript, and you should be comfortable running a Node script from a terminal. You don't need to know anything about sockets. I'll show code as I type it, I'll explain why before how, and whenever something feels like magic I'll open the browser dev tools and show you the actual bytes. If you're following along, create a folder called `scoreboard`, run `npm init -y`, and install Express and a package called `ws`. We'll use `ws` later, but it's nice to have it ready.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Let's set up the starting point so the next lecture begins with something running. Create `server.js`. We require Express, create the app, and serve a static folder called `public`. Then we define `matchState` as a plain object with `home: 'Mumbai'`, `away: 'Chennai'`, `homeScore: 0`, `awayScore: 0` and `minute: 0`. We also add a number called `version`, starting at zero, which goes up every time anything changes. Remember that `version` field. It looks like a small detail now, but in the polling and long-polling lectures it's going to be the hero.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Live Scoreboard
text: Finally the simulator. I'll write a `setInterval` that runs every three seconds. Inside it we bump `minute`, and with some random chance we add a goal to one of the teams. Every time we change anything we also do `matchState.version += 1`. Then we call `app.listen(3000)`. Start it with `node server.js`, and you should see the server listening. Nothing visible yet, but the state is changing in the background. In the next lecture we'll look at what the browser is actually allowed to do with HTTP, because that decides everything that follows.

Before we make the scoreboard live, we need to be precise about what HTTP actually promises, because every real-time technique we'll use is a workaround for one specific limitation. HTTP is a request and response protocol. The client speaks first. The server answers. And then, as far as the protocol is concerned, the conversation is over. The server has no way of saying, out of the blue, hey browser, someone just scored. It can only reply to a question that was already asked.

Let's make that concrete in our project. In `server.js` I'll add a route: `app.get('/api/score', (req, res) => res.json(matchState))`. Start the server and open `http://localhost:3000/api/score` in the browser. You get the JSON. Wait a few seconds, and you see the same page. Now refresh, and the minute has moved. The server's state changed in between, but the browser had no idea until we asked again. That is the whole problem in one picture. I'd encourage you to do this yourself rather than just watch, because seeing the stale page next to the fresh JSON makes the limitation stick.

Open the Network tab in dev tools and click on that request. Look at what's in it. There's a method, GET, a path, and a pile of request headers like `Host`, `Accept` and `User-Agent`. The response has a status line, `200 OK`, headers such as `Content-Type: application/json`, and then the body. Notice the headers are plain text and they're sent every single time. Hold that thought, because later when we measure cost, those repeated headers are going to matter a lot.

There's another thing about the contract. HTTP is stateless. Each request stands on its own, and the server isn't required to remember the previous one. That's great for scaling, because any server in a pool can answer any request. But it also means that when we say we want the server to push, there is no built-in notion of a client the server can push to. It has no list of who's listening. We'll have to invent that, either by keeping connections open or by keeping our own list.

So what are our options, given the contract? One, the client asks repeatedly, which is polling. Two, the client asks, and the server deliberately delays the answer, which is long-polling. Three, the server answers once but never finishes the response, streaming data as it goes, which is how Server-Sent Events work. Four, we ask HTTP to stop being HTTP on this connection and switch to something bidirectional, which is the WebSocket upgrade. Every technique in this course is one of those four moves.

One more detail worth knowing is that modern HTTP, versions 1.1, 2 and 3, all keep this same request and response model at the application level. HTTP/2 lets you multiplex many requests on one connection and has a feature called server push, but that was meant for sending assets early and browsers have largely removed it. It is not a general way to send live data to a page. So don't expect the newer version of HTTP to rescue us here.

Let's write down the model we'll use for the rest of this course. The client initiates, the server responds, and any liveness has to be either simulated by the client asking often, or by the server stretching out its response. In the next lecture we do the simplest possible version of that: we ask often. We'll write the polling loop in `scoreboard.js`, watch it work, and then watch it waste a surprising amount of effort.

Let's make the scoreboard actually update. The simplest idea is the one everyone reaches for first: ask the server every second. This is called short polling. Open `public/scoreboard.js`. We write an async function called `fetchScore`. Inside, we do `const res = await fetch('/api/score')`, then `const state = await res.json()`, and we call a function `render(state)` that writes the team names and the scores into the DOM. Nothing special. Then at the bottom we write `setInterval(fetchScore, 1000)`.

Open the page, and it works. Numbers tick, goals appear within a second or so. For a first version, that's honestly fine, and I want you to respect that. A lot of production dashboards run on exactly this. It's simple, it works through every proxy and firewall, it needs no special server code, and it's easy to debug because each poll is just a normal request you can see in the Network tab. That matters, because the best technique is the simplest one that meets your requirements, and we should know exactly when it stops meeting them.

But now look at that Network tab while the page is open for a minute. Sixty requests. Now ask yourself how many of them carried new information. The simulator changes things every three seconds and goals are rare, so most of those responses are identical to the one before. We are sending a full request, with all its headers, and receiving a full JSON body, just to be told nothing changed. Multiply that by ten thousand viewers and your server is handling ten thousand requests per second for a scoreboard that changes once every few seconds.

We can already reduce the waste a little using our `version` number. Change the fetch to `/api/score?since=${lastVersion}`. On the server, if `req.query.since` equals the current `version`, we respond with `res.status(204).end()`, meaning no content. The browser still makes the trip, but the response is tiny. In `scoreboard.js` we only call `render` if the status is 200, and we store the new version. You've saved bandwidth, but you haven't saved the requests themselves, and you haven't saved any server work per request. This is a cheap trick, and it's worth having in your toolbox even if you never move beyond polling.

Now the other side of the trade. Updates are late by up to the polling interval. With a one-second interval, a goal can show up anywhere from zero to one second after it happened, so on average half a second late. If you drop the interval to 100 milliseconds to feel more live, you multiply the request load by ten. That's the fundamental tension in short polling: freshness and cost are tied together, and you can only buy one with the other.

So where does short polling make sense? When updates are infrequent and delay is acceptable, like checking whether a long export job has finished, or refreshing a dashboard every thirty seconds. Where it hurts is anything that wants to feel instant. Try this as a small experiment: set the interval to 200 milliseconds, open the page in five tabs, and watch the server's request log fly. In the next lecture we fix the waste in a smarter way, by making the server hold the request instead of answering instantly.

Long-polling keeps the polling idea but flips who waits. Instead of the client asking every second and mostly hearing "nothing new", the client asks once, and the server holds that request open until it actually has something to say. When there's an update, the server answers. The client immediately asks again. From the browser's point of view it's still plain HTTP, but updates now arrive the moment they happen, not on the next tick of a timer.

Let's build it. In `server.js` we need somewhere to park the waiting requests. I'll declare `const waiting = []` near the top. Then add a route, `app.get('/poll', ...)`. Inside, read `const since = Number(req.query.since)`. If `matchState.version` is already greater than `since`, we answer right away with `res.json(matchState)`, because the client is behind and should catch up. Otherwise we push the response object into `waiting`, and we don't call `res.json` yet. The request just sits there.

Now we need to release them. Wherever the simulator changes state, after we bump `version`, we add a loop: `while (waiting.length) { waiting.pop().json(matchState) }`. All the parked requests finally get the new state. But there's one more thing we need, a timeout, because proxies and browsers don't like requests that never finish. So when we park a response, we also start a timer with `setTimeout`, say 25 seconds, and when it fires we remove the response from `waiting` and send `res.status(204).end()`. The client treats a 204 as "nothing yet, ask again".

Now the client. In `scoreboard.js` we replace the interval with a loop. I'll write `async function poll() { while (true) { ... } }`. Inside, we try `fetch('/poll?since=' + lastVersion)`. If the status is 200, we parse the JSON, render, and update `lastVersion`. If it's 204, we just continue and ask again. And in a `catch`, we wait a second before retrying so a dead server doesn't make us spin in a tight loop. Notice there's no timer for freshness anymore. The loop is the heartbeat.

Run it. Open the Network tab and you'll see something different: a single request sitting in the pending state, sometimes for twenty seconds. Then a goal happens, the request completes in a flash, and a new one starts. Updates now show up essentially the instant the server has them. That's a big improvement over short polling, and it's why long-polling powered a whole generation of chat apps and notification systems before WebSockets existed. Keep that picture in your head, because it's the mental model for everything else in this chapter.

But be honest about what's still happening. Every update costs a complete HTTP response and a new request, with all the headers again. Between the response arriving and the next request landing there's a small gap where the server has no parked request for that client, and updates in that gap have to be caught by that `since` version check. That's why the version number matters so much: without it you'd lose events in the gap. We'll come back to these costs with real numbers. First, though, let's look at what a truly persistent connection looks like, starting with the header that makes the switch happen.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: We've seen how far plain HTTP can be stretched. Now let's look at the mechanism that lets us leave it behind, because the WebSocket protocol doesn't start from nothing. It starts as an ordinary HTTP request, and the header that turns it into something else is called Upgrade. In this lecture we'll learn what that header means in HTTP itself, which is bigger than WebSockets, and then we'll watch it in our scoreboard. Think of this lecture as the doorway between the first chapter of the course and everything that follows, so it's worth getting the picture crisp.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: HTTP/1.1 has a general feature: a client can send a request that includes `Connection: Upgrade` and an `Upgrade` header naming a protocol it would like to speak instead. The server has three choices. It can ignore the header and answer normally. It can refuse. Or it can reply with the status `101 Switching Protocols`, and from that point on the very same TCP connection stops carrying HTTP and carries whatever protocol was agreed. WebSocket is the most famous user of this, but the mechanism is generic.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Why does it work this way, instead of WebSockets just opening a fresh connection on a new port? Because of the real world. Port 80 and port 443 are open almost everywhere. Corporate firewalls, hotel Wi-Fi, mobile carriers, they all let HTTP traffic through. If WebSockets had required a new port, a huge fraction of users simply couldn't connect. Starting as HTTP means the connection passes through the same infrastructure, reuses existing cookies and authentication, and goes through the same TLS setup as any other secure request.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Let's see it with our own eyes, without any browser. In the terminal I'll run curl against a server that doesn't understand WebSockets yet, our existing Express app. The command is `curl -i -H "Connection: Upgrade" -H "Upgrade: websocket" http://localhost:3000/`. The `-i` flag shows the response headers. Our server just ignores the upgrade request and replies `200 OK` with the HTML page. That's the first choice I mentioned: a server that doesn't know the protocol answers as if the header wasn't there.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: That detail is actually important for design. An upgrade is a request, not a command. The client is asking, and any server along the path is allowed to say no. This is also why, when you debug a WebSocket that mysteriously fails to connect, the first question is always whether something in the middle, like a load balancer, an nginx config or a corporate proxy, stripped or rejected those two headers. We'll see a lot of failures that look like WebSocket bugs but are really Upgrade failures.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Now let's prepare the server side for the next lecture. In `server.js` I'll change how we start things. Instead of calling `app.listen` and discarding the result, we write `const server = app.listen(3000)`, keeping the HTTP server object. That object emits an event called `upgrade` whenever a client sends an Upgrade request. I'll add `server.on('upgrade', (req, socket, head) => { console.log('upgrade asked for', req.headers.upgrade) })`. Notice that the `socket` is the raw TCP socket. We are below Express now, before any response object exists.

lecture_title: 2.1 - The Upgrade Header: Asking HTTP to Switch Protocols
text: Start the server again and rerun that curl command. This time you'll see our log line print `upgrade asked for websocket`, and the curl hangs, because we received the upgrade request and haven't answered it. That's exactly the gap we're going to fill in the next lecture, where we write the handshake response by hand. It's a good one to do manually once, because after that you'll never wonder what the `ws` library is hiding from you.

So let's talk about what actually happens at the start of a WebSocket connection. I'll explain it first and then we'll write the server side of it by hand in `server.js`. A WebSocket connection begins with something called the handshake, and it starts as a regular HTTP request. The browser sends a GET request to the server but includes a special header: Upgrade: websocket. It also includes a Sec-WebSocket-Key header which is a randomly generated base64-encoded value. The browser is essentially asking the server to upgrade this HTTP connection to a persistent WebSocket connection. This is why WebSocket URLs start with ws:// or wss:// but the initial handshake itself travels over HTTP.

Let's see that in the browser, because it's much clearer when you can look at it. In the page's console I'll type `new WebSocket('ws://localhost:3000/live')`. It will fail, since our server doesn't answer the handshake yet, but that's useful: open the Network tab, filter by WS, and click the failed request. You'll see the request headers exactly as described. `Connection: Upgrade`, `Upgrade: websocket`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`, and the `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, which looks like twenty-four characters of random base64. Version 13 is the version everybody uses, so you can treat that header as a constant.

Now the server's turn. Here is the part that people find mysterious, so I'll go slowly. When the server receives the upgrade request it responds with HTTP 101 Switching Protocols. It takes the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key, concatenates a fixed GUID string to it, hashes the result with SHA-1, and base64 encodes it. This becomes the Sec-WebSocket-Accept response header. The client verifies this value to confirm it is talking to a genuine WebSocket server and not a misconfigured proxy. Once the 101 response is received, the HTTP connection is upgraded and both sides can now send frames in either direction at any time without the request-response overhead of HTTP.

Let me say why that exchange exists at all, since it feels like an odd dance. The key and accept values are not security in the sense of authentication or encryption. Their job is to prove that the server really understood the WebSocket protocol, and that this isn't a cached or confused HTTP response being mistaken for one. That's all it proves. It also stops a normal web page from tricking a non-WebSocket server into acting like one, because a page can't control those headers freely.

Okay, now we write it. In `server.js` we require the `crypto` module. The fixed GUID is the string `258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`, and it's defined in the protocol specification, RFC 6455, so don't try to change it. In our `upgrade` handler we read `const key = req.headers['sec-websocket-key']`. Then `const accept = crypto.createHash('sha1').update(key + GUID).digest('base64')`. That one line is the entire trick: concatenate, SHA-1, base64. You can find the same constant in every language's WebSocket library, which is a nice sanity check that we're not making anything up here.

Then we write the response straight onto the socket. I'll call `socket.write` with a string made of the status line `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`, then `Upgrade: websocket`, then `Connection: Upgrade`, then `Sec-WebSocket-Accept:` followed by our `accept` value, and finally an empty line, meaning a carriage return and line feed twice at the end. That blank line matters. Without it the browser keeps waiting for more headers. Now try the same `new WebSocket` call in the console again.

This time the Network tab shows a status of 101, and the console shows no error. We have a connection. And here's the moment I want you to think about: what happens next. After the WebSocket handshake completes, the connection becomes a full-duplex channel. Unlike HTTP where the client must always initiate a request, with WebSocket the server can push data to the client at any time. Data is sent in frames rather than complete HTTP messages, which makes it much more efficient for real-time applications like chat, live dashboards, or collaborative editing. The connection stays open until either side explicitly closes it with a close frame, or the network drops.

For now our server doesn't read or write anything after the handshake, so the connection just sits open. In the next lecture we'll look at what those frames look like on the wire, how big they are, and how to read one byte by byte. Before we move on, one reflection exercise: take the `Sec-WebSocket-Key` from your own request, compute the accept value with a small Node script, and check that it matches what our server sent.

Last lecture ended with an open connection and nothing flowing over it. Now let's look at what actually travels. After the 101 response, HTTP is finished on this socket. What we exchange are frames, and understanding the frame format is what turns WebSockets from magic into something you could implement on a weekend. We won't implement all of it, but we'll read real frames out of our scoreboard server, and I think that makes everything else feel solid.

Here's the structure, starting with the first byte. The top bit is called FIN, and it says whether this frame is the final fragment of a message. Large messages can be split across several frames, and FIN is how the receiver knows when the last piece has arrived. Then there are three reserved bits, which are zero unless an extension like compression is negotiated. And the lower four bits of that first byte are the opcode, which says what kind of frame this is.

The opcodes you need to know are short. Opcode `0x1` is a text frame, with UTF-8 payload. Opcode `0x2` is binary. Opcode `0x0` is a continuation, meaning more of the same message is coming. Then there are control frames: `0x8` is close, `0x9` is ping, and `0xA` is pong. Control frames are small, at most 125 bytes, and they can't be fragmented. Ping and pong are going to be central when we talk about heartbeats later in the course, so remember that they live at the protocol level, below your messages.

The second byte holds a bit called MASK, and then the payload length in seven bits. If the length is 125 or less, that's the length, and we're done. If it's 126, the next two bytes hold the real length as a 16-bit number. If it's 127, the next eight bytes hold it as a 64-bit number. So a tiny scoreboard update, say 40 bytes of JSON, costs just two bytes of header from the server, and six from the browser. Compare that with a few hundred bytes of HTTP headers on every poll.

Now the masking, which surprises people. Every frame that a browser sends to a server must be masked. The sender picks a random four-byte masking key, puts it in the frame, and XORs each payload byte with the key, cycling through its four bytes. Frames from server to client are not masked. Why? It isn't encryption, because the key travels right there in the frame. It exists to stop badly behaved proxies from confusing a WebSocket payload with an HTTP request, which could poison caches. The browser handles all of this for you.

Let's decode one by hand. In `server.js` inside the `upgrade` handler, after writing the 101, I'll add `socket.on('data', (buf) => { ... })`. Inside, I read `const opcode = buf[0] & 0x0f`, `const masked = (buf[1] & 0x80) !== 0`, and `let len = buf[1] & 0x7f`. For short messages the mask key is `buf.slice(2, 6)` and the payload starts at byte six. Then a loop does `payload[i] = buf[6 + i] ^ mask[i % 4]`. Convert with `toString('utf8')` and log it.

From the browser console, once the socket is open, I can call `ws.send('hello')` and our server logs `hello`. We've just parsed a real WebSocket frame by hand. It's rough, since it ignores fragmentation and large lengths, so in practice we'll hand this job to the `ws` package. But now you know what's inside it. You also now know why a WebSocket message of ten bytes is vastly cheaper than an HTTP request carrying the same ten bytes, and we'll quantify that in the next chapter.

We've been poking at WebSockets from the console. Now let's use the browser WebSocket API properly, from `scoreboard.js`, and switch our server to the `ws` package so we can stop parsing bytes. First the server. At the top of `server.js` I'll write `const { WebSocketServer } = require('ws')`. Then, instead of our hand-written upgrade handler, `const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server, path: '/live' })`. That attaches to the same HTTP server and handles the handshake we just wrote, including the key hashing and the 101 response.

Next, what the server does on a connection. `wss.on('connection', (ws) => { ws.send(JSON.stringify(matchState)) })`. Every time a client connects, we send it the current state immediately, so it never has to wait for the next goal to see a score. Then in the simulator, after we bump `version`, we loop over `wss.clients` and, for each client whose `readyState` equals `WebSocket.OPEN`, we call `client.send(JSON.stringify(matchState))`. That's our whole broadcast. Compare that with the waiting list in long-polling. There's no parked request to find and no timeout to manage.

Now the browser side, which is gloriously small. In `scoreboard.js` I'll replace the polling loop with `const socket = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:3000/live')`. When deployed over HTTPS you must use `wss://`, because browsers block insecure WebSockets from secure pages. Then we attach handlers. `socket.onopen` can just log that we connected. And `socket.onmessage = (event) => { render(JSON.parse(event.data)) }`. That's it. The `event.data` is a string for text frames, and by default a Blob for binary, which you can change using `socket.binaryType`.

Let me point out the lifecycle, because beginners trip on it. A socket has a `readyState`: 0 is CONNECTING, 1 is OPEN, 2 is CLOSING, and 3 is CLOSED. You can only call `send` when it's 1, otherwise you get an error, so if your code might send early, check the state or queue the message. The events are `open`, `message`, `error`, and `close`. Notice that `error` carries almost no detail on purpose, and the `close` event has a `code` and a `reason` that tell you more.

Let's also make it two-way, since that's the real advantage. I'll add a small button on the page called Cheer. Its click handler runs `socket.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'cheer' }))`. On the server we add `ws.on('message', (data) => { ... })`, parse it, and when the type is `cheer` we increment a counter and broadcast the new count to everybody. The client never sends a new HTTP request, and the server never needs to be asked. Open two browser windows, click Cheer in one, and watch it update in the other.

To close cleanly, call `socket.close(1000, 'done')`. Code 1000 means normal closure, and the server's `close` handler fires with that code. If the server dies or the network drops, you'll see code 1006 instead, which means the connection closed abnormally and there was no close frame. Keep that in mind, because in the resilience chapter we'll use close codes to decide whether to reconnect. For now, our scoreboard is live over a WebSocket. Next chapter, we're going to compare it against long-polling honestly, because it isn't always the right answer.

Now we have two real-time versions of the scoreboard, long-polling and WebSockets, and the obvious question is which one you should use. Let's compare them properly, starting with a short history, because it explains why long-polling exists at all. I'll keep it conceptual in this lecture, and in the lecture after next we'll measure it with our own code. By the end of it you should be able to defend your choice to a teammate, with reasons rather than habit. That's the skill I care about, more than any one API.

Rewind to the years before WebSockets were widely supported. Developers wanted chat, notifications and live feeds, and the browser offered exactly one tool: HTTP requests. So they made it work. Before WebSockets, the common trick for real-time updates was long-polling. The client sends an HTTP request and the server deliberately holds it open instead of responding immediately. When data becomes available, the server responds, and the client instantly sends another request to wait again. It simulates a push, but every message still pays the full cost of an HTTP request and response — new headers, sometimes a new TCP connection — and there is always a gap between responses where the client is reconnecting.
