Let's map that onto our scoreboard code. In the long-polling version, each update meant the `/poll` response completed, the client ran `render`, and a new `fetch` started. That fetch needs headers, cookies if you have any, and potentially a fresh TCP and TLS handshake if the old connection was closed by some intermediate server. The gap I just mentioned is the time between those two. If a goal and a foul land in that gap, the server has to hold both until the next request arrives, which is exactly why we built that `version` check.

Now the other side of the comparison. A WebSocket replaces all of that with a single long-lived, full-duplex TCP connection. After the initial HTTP Upgrade handshake, both sides can send frames at any time with only a few bytes of framing overhead — no repeated headers, no reconnect gap. This makes WebSockets dramatically more efficient for high-frequency, bidirectional traffic like chat, live cursors, or trading data. Long-polling still has its place: it is simpler, works through old proxies, and is fine for low-frequency updates where a dedicated connection per client would be wasteful.

Let me give you a way to think about this that I use in real projects. Ask three questions. How often do updates happen? Do messages flow in both directions? And how many clients will be connected at the same time? A scoreboard that changes every few seconds, shown to many viewers, who never send anything back, is a one-direction low-frequency flow. A multiplayer cursor that moves sixty times a second in both directions is the opposite.

There are also practical constraints that don't show up in benchmarks. A WebSocket needs your infrastructure to support the Upgrade handshake, so load balancers need configuring for it, and sticky routing or a shared message layer becomes necessary when you run more than one server process. Long-polling is plain HTTP, so it works with anything that handles HTTP. And a held connection costs memory on the server either way, so neither is free in a big deployment. We'll look at that in a moment.

Let me also warn you about a common mistake. People hear that WebSockets are faster, and they replace everything with them, including features that are just occasional notifications. Then they own reconnect logic, heartbeats, authentication on a long-lived socket, and scaling a stateful connection layer, to deliver a message once an hour. WebSockets are the right tool when the traffic justifies the complexity. For many apps the honest answer is a simpler option, and the next lecture introduces one of them.

So here's the summary I want you to leave with. Long-polling simulates push on top of request and response, and pays per message. WebSockets give a persistent, full-duplex channel and pay mostly at connection time. Neither is better in the abstract, and the right choice depends on frequency, direction and scale. In the next lecture we meet Server-Sent Events, which sits in the middle: push from the server over ordinary HTTP, without the upgrade.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: There's a transport I deliberately left until now, because it fits between the two we've compared, and for our scoreboard it might actually be the best fit. It's called Server-Sent Events, or SSE. The idea is simple. The browser makes an ordinary HTTP GET request. The server answers with a status 200, but it never finishes the response. It keeps writing text to it, whenever it has something to say, and the browser delivers each piece to your code as an event.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: The browser gives you a built-in class for it, called `EventSource`. In `scoreboard.js` I'll write `const source = new EventSource('/events')`. Then `source.onmessage = (event) => { render(JSON.parse(event.data)) }`. There's no manual reading loop, no JSON streaming parser, and no reconnect code, because the browser handles reconnection for you. If the connection drops, `EventSource` waits a few seconds and connects again automatically. That's a lot of resilience for free. Honestly, when I first saw how little code this was, I wondered why I had ever bothered hand-rolling a long-polling loop for notification features.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: Now the server. In `server.js` we add `app.get('/events', (req, res) => { ... })`. First, headers: `res.set({ 'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream', 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache', Connection: 'keep-alive' })`, and then `res.flushHeaders()` so the browser sees the response begin right away. Then we keep a set called `sseClients`, add `res` to it, and when the request closes, via `req.on('close')`, we remove it. That mirrors the waiting list from long-polling, except we never empty it on each message. Notice also that we call `res.write` and never `res.end`, because ending the response would end the stream.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: The format on the wire is plain text, and that's the beautiful thing about it. A message is one or more lines starting with `data:`, followed by a blank line. So to send our state, we write `res.write('data: ' + JSON.stringify(matchState) + '\n\n')`. The double newline ends the message. You can also add an `id:` line, and an `event:` line to name a custom event type so you can listen with `source.addEventListener('goal', ...)` instead of `onmessage`. A line starting with a colon is a comment, which is handy as a keep-alive.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: Here's the feature that makes SSE shine for our `version` idea. If you send `id: 42` with a message, the browser remembers it. When it reconnects after a drop, it automatically sends a request header called `Last-Event-ID: 42`. On the server we read `req.headers['last-event-id']` and send anything we missed. So the same version trick we hand-built for polling is part of the protocol. You can also set the delay before reconnecting by sending a line like `retry: 3000`.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: What are the limits? SSE is one-way, server to client. If the page needs to send something, it uses a normal `fetch` POST, which is fine for a scoreboard where the only thing going up is an occasional vote. It carries text only, no binary. And on HTTP/1.1 browsers allow only about six simultaneous connections per domain, so six tabs of SSE can starve your page of requests, though HTTP/2 lifts that limit by multiplexing. Also watch out for proxies that buffer responses, which delays events until a buffer fills.

lecture_title: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP
text: So for the scoreboard, think about what we really need. Updates flow one way, they are small, they're occasional, and we want automatic reconnect with catch-up. SSE gives all that over plain HTTP, with no upgrade, no custom frames and less code than either of our earlier versions. It's very often the best answer for live feeds, notifications and progress bars, and I'd rather you pick it for those than reach for WebSockets by reflex. In the next lecture we measure all four honestly.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: We've been saying things like "WebSockets are more efficient" and "polling wastes requests." Today we stop asserting and start measuring. We'll build a tiny benchmark harness for the scoreboard that counts three things for each transport: bytes on the wire, latency from event to screen, and open connections on the server. The numbers won't be identical on your machine, but the shapes will be, and the shapes are what teach you. Treat this as an engineering habit, because a claim about performance that you haven't measured is really just an opinion.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: Let's start with bytes. In `server.js` I'll add a small counter object called `stats` with a field `bytesOut`, and a helper called `send(res, payload)` that adds the payload length before writing. For the HTTP-based versions I also want header cost, so I use the `Content-Length` and add an estimated header size of about 250 bytes per response. That's a conservative figure for a request and response pair with typical headers, and real apps with cookies are much bigger, often a kilobyte or more. You can adjust that header estimate and rerun, and the conclusion won't flip, which is why I'm comfortable using a rough number.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: Now run a scenario. One scoreboard update every three seconds, one minute, one client. Short polling at one request per second sends sixty responses, almost all just 204 or an unchanged state, each with its headers. Long-polling sends roughly twenty, one per update, each with headers plus a new request. SSE sends twenty tiny `data:` messages of about fifty bytes each, plus the headers once. WebSocket sends the same twenty messages with two bytes of framing each, plus the handshake once.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: When you print the totals, the ordering is very consistent. Short polling is by far the heaviest, perhaps fifteen to twenty kilobytes for that minute. Long-polling is a fraction of that, but still pays headers on every message. SSE and WebSockets are both roughly just the payload, around a kilobyte. This is where my earlier point about the header size lands: for tiny messages sent often, the HTTP envelope is bigger than the message, and persistent connections win by an order of magnitude.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: Next, latency. I'll add a `sentAt` timestamp to every message the simulator broadcasts, and in `scoreboard.js` compute `Date.now() - state.sentAt` when we render, which works since both run on my machine's clock. Short polling shows an average delay near half the interval, so about five hundred milliseconds. Long-polling, SSE and WebSockets all arrive within a few milliseconds locally. Over a real network they differ by the usual round trip, and long-polling adds another round trip whenever it has to open a new connection.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: The third measure is the one people forget: open connections and memory. Add `app.get('/stats', ...)` returning counts, with `waiting.length`, `sseClients.size` and `wss.clients.size`. Then use a small script with a loop that opens a thousand clients of one type. You'll find that a held connection is cheap in Node, a few kilobytes each, so a single process can hold tens of thousands, but short polling costs CPU instead, because every poll runs your request handler. The cost moves from memory to compute.

lecture_title: 3.3 - Measuring the Cost: Bytes, Latency and Open Connections
text: So here's what the measurements tell us. Short polling spends bandwidth and CPU for freshness you may not need. Long-polling is fine for low frequency and badly shaped for high frequency. SSE and WebSockets are the efficient ones, and the deciding factor between them is direction. Do you need to send from the client constantly? Pick WebSockets. If it's mostly server push, SSE is simpler. Now we have all the data to decide. Next, we'll make whichever one we choose survive a bad network.

Welcome to the resilience chapter. Everything we've built so far works beautifully on localhost, and that is exactly the problem. Real networks drop. A phone goes into a tunnel, a laptop sleeps, a deploy restarts your server, a load balancer closes an idle connection after a minute. A live scoreboard that freezes silently when this happens is worse than one that never updated at all, because users trust the numbers. So in this chapter we make the connection keep itself alive, starting with reconnecting.

Let's see the failure first. With the WebSocket version running, stop the server in the terminal with Control C and look at the page. The socket's `onclose` fires, with code 1006, and nothing else happens. The scoreboard just sits there with stale numbers. Now restart the server, and the page is still dead, because a WebSocket object can't be reopened. A closed socket is finished. To reconnect, we have to create a brand new `WebSocket`, so we need to wrap the creation in a function we can call again.

In `scoreboard.js` I'll restructure. I write `let socket` and a function `connect()` that does `socket = new WebSocket(url)` and attaches our handlers. In `socket.onclose` we call `setTimeout(connect, 1000)`. That's a first reconnect, and it works: kill the server, restart it, and the page recovers by itself within a second. Great. But this naive version has a nasty failure mode that I want you to understand, because it has taken down real systems. Try it yourself before moving on, since the restructure is only a few lines and it makes the next steps much easier to follow.

Imagine the server is down for a minute, or the server is up but overloaded. Ten thousand clients all lose connection at the same moment, and every one retries every second. The moment the server comes back, ten thousand handshakes arrive together. That overwhelms it, it fails again, all of them disconnect again, and they all retry at the same instant again. This is called a thundering herd, and a fixed retry interval makes it worse, because the clients stay synchronized with each other.

The standard fix has two ingredients. The first is exponential backoff: after each failed attempt, wait longer than before. Something like one second, then two, then four, then eight, doubling each time, up to a maximum such as thirty seconds. The second is jitter: add randomness so the clients spread out instead of marching in lockstep. Backoff reduces the load during a long outage, and jitter prevents the retries from synchronizing in the first place.

Here's the code. I'll add `let attempts = 0` at the top. In `onclose` we compute `const base = Math.min(30000, 1000 * Math.pow(2, attempts))`, and then the delay is `Math.random() * base`, which is the technique often called full jitter. We do `attempts += 1` and `setTimeout(connect, delay)`. And in `socket.onopen` we reset with `attempts = 0`, so a healthy connection forgets its history. Without that reset, a client that reconnected successfully an hour ago would still wait thirty seconds after its next blip.

Now one more detail: reconnecting is not just opening a socket. While we were disconnected, goals may have happened. In `onopen`, our server already sends the full `matchState` as the first message, which fixes the scoreboard because we send complete state. But for event streams, such as a chat, you need to send the last version you saw, as we did with `since`, so the server can replay what you missed. So remember the rule for any live feature: the reconnect protocol is part of the design, not an afterthought. Next lecture, the harder problem: noticing a connection that died without telling you.

Last time we handled connections that close. The sneakier case is a connection that dies without closing. Think about a laptop's Wi-Fi switching off, or a phone entering a dead zone, or a router in the middle silently dropping the mapping for your connection. No FIN packet and no close frame ever arrives. As far as the browser's TCP stack knows, the connection is still open, and it can take minutes, sometimes much longer, to notice. Your scoreboard looks connected, and it's frozen.

Let me say precisely why, because it's a basic property of TCP. A TCP connection is just agreed-upon state at both ends. If one end vanishes without sending anything, the other end has no way to know until it tries to send something and doesn't get acknowledgements, and then retransmission timeouts take a long time. If nobody's sending, nobody ever finds out. So an idle connection that has quietly died is indistinguishable from an idle connection that's healthy. To tell the difference, you have to send something and expect a reply.

That's what a heartbeat is. Every so often, one side sends a small message, and the other side must answer in a short time. If the answer doesn't come, the connection is considered dead. The WebSocket protocol builds this in: remember the ping opcode, `0x9`, and the pong opcode, `0xA`. When one side receives a ping, it must reply with a pong carrying the same payload. Browsers do this automatically for you, so you never write code to answer a ping.

On the server, the `ws` library gives us what we need. Inside the `connection` handler I'll set `ws.isAlive = true`, and add `ws.on('pong', () => { ws.isAlive = true })`. Then I add a `setInterval` that runs every thirty seconds and loops over `wss.clients`. For each client, if `ws.isAlive` is false, we call `ws.terminate()`, which destroys the connection immediately. Otherwise we set `ws.isAlive = false` and call `ws.ping()`. Next round, anything that hasn't answered with a pong is dropped.

This does two useful jobs at once. It detects dead clients, so our server doesn't accumulate zombie sockets holding memory. And the traffic itself keeps the connection active, which matters because many proxies and load balancers close connections that stay silent for too long, often around sixty seconds. A ping every thirty seconds keeps those middle boxes happy. Many people only find out about this in production, when connections get dropped at suspiciously exact intervals.

Now here's the browser's blind spot. The browser WebSocket API gives your JavaScript no way to send a ping or see a pong. The browser handles protocol pings invisibly. So if you want the client to detect a dead server, you need an application-level heartbeat. I'll add it in `scoreboard.js`: the server sends `{ type: 'tick' }` messages every ten seconds, and the client keeps `lastSeen = Date.now()`. A timer checks every five seconds, and if more than twenty-five seconds passed with nothing, we call `socket.close()`, which triggers our reconnect-with-backoff path.

So now we have both directions covered. The server uses protocol pings to prune dead clients and keep proxies awake. The client uses an application-level tick to notice a silent server and reconnect. Tune the intervals to your environment, since mobile networks want longer ones to save battery. Then there's one more resilience problem that appears when connections are alive but slow, which is when the server writes faster than the client can read. That's backpressure, and it's the next lecture.

Here's a failure that doesn't involve the network dropping at all. The connection is alive and healthy, but the receiver is slower than the sender. Maybe it's a phone on a bad cellular link, or a browser tab that's busy. Our simulator sends scoreboard updates, and the `send` call returns immediately regardless. But the bytes have to go somewhere, and if the client can't take them fast enough they pile up in a buffer in memory. That pile is what backpressure is about.

Let me make it visible. I'll add a stress mode to our simulator, which broadcasts an update every ten milliseconds. On the client, I'll deliberately slow things down: in `onmessage` I run a busy loop for fifty milliseconds. Now the server produces a hundred messages per second and the client can consume twenty. The extra eighty per second have to wait. On the browser side, they queue up inside the browser's networking layer. On the server side, in `ws`, if the operating system's socket buffer is full, they queue in Node's memory.

The tool for seeing this is a property called `bufferedAmount`. On the browser WebSocket it tells you how many bytes you've passed to `send` that haven't yet been transmitted to the network. For the `ws` library on the server, the same name exists on each socket. So on the server I can log `ws.bufferedAmount` for each client in the broadcast loop. When you run the stress test you'll see it climb for the slow client and stay near zero for fast ones. If you ignore it, your Node process's memory grows steadily until it falls over.

What do we do about it? The simplest policy for a scoreboard is to skip. Before sending to a client, check `if (client.bufferedAmount > 64 * 1024) continue`. The client is behind, so we don't make it worse, and since each message carries the whole `matchState`, the next message that does get through brings them fully up to date. That's called load shedding, and it's valid whenever messages are snapshots instead of deltas, where the latest value replaces everything before it.

For event-style messages, where each one matters, such as chat lines or trades, skipping isn't acceptable. There you have a few choices. Slow down the producer, by pausing a source until the buffer drains. Queue per client with a limit, and when the limit is crossed, drop the oldest messages or disconnect the client, which forces it to reconnect and resync from a known version. Disconnecting a hopelessly slow consumer is often the right call, because one slow client shouldn't be able to consume the memory that everyone shares.

The same idea applies in the browser when you send. If your page streams large uploads or rapid cursor positions with `socket.send`, check `socket.bufferedAmount` first and hold off while it's high, using a short timer to try again. It's the browser's version of the same flow control we added on the server. And also note what's different with TCP itself: TCP has built-in flow control, but the WebSocket API doesn't expose it directly, which is why this property exists.

Let's connect the three lessons of this chapter. Reconnect with backoff and jitter so an outage doesn't become a stampede. Use heartbeats so a silent death becomes a detected one. And watch `bufferedAmount` so a slow reader can't hurt the system. Those three together are what separate a demo from something you'd put in front of real users. In the last chapter, we take everything we've built and decide, feature by feature, which transport to ship.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: For the final project step, I want to answer the question we've been circling the whole course: what do we actually ship? We have a scoreboard with four working transports. Shipping all four would be silly, so let's decide the way you'd decide at work, by going through the features of the product and picking the lightest transport that meets each need. The principle I'll use is simple: choose the simplest technology that meets the requirement, and only escalate when you can name the reason.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature one is the live score and match clock, which is what the whole course started with. The data flows from server to client only. It changes every few seconds. It has to survive reconnects, and it should catch up on missed updates. That's a textbook case for Server-Sent Events. We get automatic reconnects, we get `Last-Event-ID` for catch-up, we pass through ordinary HTTP infrastructure, and we write the least code. So the scoreboard's main feed becomes `/events`.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature two is match commentary, short text lines that appear as they're written by a journalist. Same shape: one direction, low frequency, important not to miss messages. Another good fit for SSE, and in fact it can share the same stream with a custom `event: commentary` type, so the page listens with `source.addEventListener('commentary', ...)`. One connection, multiple event types. There's no reason to open a second connection for this. That is a good example of not multiplying connections when one will do, because every open connection has a cost on the server and on a phone's battery.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature three is the crowd reactions panel, where thousands of fans send emoji cheers in real time and everyone sees a live count. Now traffic goes both ways and it's frequent, so this is where a WebSocket pays for itself. We keep our `/live` endpoint with the heartbeats and backpressure rules from the last chapter, and use load shedding, since the count is a snapshot. A reasonable detail: the server aggregates cheers and broadcasts the totals once per second, instead of rebroadcasting every single click.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Feature four is the admin console that edits the score. This is a rare action, only a few times in a match, sent by one trusted person. A plain `fetch` POST to `/api/score` is perfect. It's easy to authenticate, easy to retry, easy to log, and gives a clear success or error. Putting this on a socket would add complexity and give nothing. And what about long-polling and short polling? We keep short polling as a fallback for ancient environments, and a status page that refreshes every thirty seconds is a good use of it.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: Let's look at the final structure in code. `server.js` now has four things: a REST route for admin updates, an `/events` SSE endpoint, a `/live` WebSocket endpoint, and a `/health` route that a load balancer can poll. A single function called `publish(change)` updates `matchState`, bumps `version`, and fans out to SSE clients and WebSocket clients together. That's the nice thing about having built these separately: the transports became thin layers over one shared state and one shared version number.

lecture_title: 5.1 - Shipping the Scoreboard: One Transport per Feature
text: A few deployment notes. Behind nginx or a cloud load balancer, SSE needs response buffering turned off, and WebSockets need the Upgrade headers passed through and an idle timeout longer than your heartbeat. Use `wss://` and HTTPS everywhere. If you run more than one server process, you'll need a shared channel such as Redis pub/sub so that a change on one instance reaches clients on the others. We won't build that here, but now you know exactly which problem it solves.

So that's the course. Let's take a few minutes to pull it together, because I want you to leave with a mental map you can reuse and not just a pile of code. We started with one limitation: in HTTP, the client asks and the server answers, and the server can't speak first. Every technique we built was a different answer to that limitation, and each one had a price that we measured rather than guessed.

Short polling asks often and pays in wasted requests. Long-polling holds the request open and pays a full HTTP exchange per message, with a gap while the client reconnects. Server-Sent Events keep one response open and stream text over it, one direction, with reconnect and catch-up built into the browser. WebSockets cross the Upgrade boundary, replace HTTP with frames, and give you a full-duplex channel at the cost of owning more of the lifecycle yourself.

Let me also revisit the handshake, because it's the heart of the course. A client sends a GET with `Upgrade: websocket` and a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`. The server answers `101 Switching Protocols` with a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` computed by appending the protocol's fixed GUID, hashing with SHA-1, and base64 encoding. After that, frames flow, opcodes tell you what each one is, and browser frames are masked. If you can explain those three sentences to a colleague, you understand WebSockets better than most people who use them.

And the resilience chapter might be the part that serves you the longest. Exponential backoff with jitter, so a mass disconnect doesn't become a stampede. Heartbeats, because a dead connection looks identical to an idle one until you test it. And `bufferedAmount`, because a slow reader will quietly eat your memory if you let it. Whatever transport you choose in a future project, those three habits transfer directly. If you only keep one chapter's worth of notes from this course, I'd keep that one.

Where should you go from here? There are some natural next steps. Try scaling the scoreboard to two server processes and add Redis pub/sub, so you feel the multi-instance problem first-hand. Look at Socket.IO, which wraps WebSockets with rooms, acknowledgements and a long-polling fallback, and see which of the things we built by hand it does for you. Read RFC 6455, the WebSocket specification, which is surprisingly readable now that you know the vocabulary. Pick one of them and spend an evening on it, because a small experiment teaches more than any amount of reading.

Also worth exploring are the newer pieces. WebTransport, built on HTTP/3, offers multiple streams and unreliable datagrams for cases where WebSockets' single ordered stream is a bottleneck, though browser support is still developing. And if you're doing server-to-server work, look at gRPC streaming. Don't adopt them because they're new. Ask the same questions we asked all course: which direction, how often, how many clients, and what happens when the network fails. They solve real problems, but only the problems they were designed for.

One last piece of advice. Build the smallest thing that works, measure it, and let the measurements tell you when to escalate. You've now built the same feature four ways, so you won't be guessing. Take the scoreboard, give it a second sport, break the network with your browser's offline mode, and see if it recovers on its own. Thanks for working through this with me, and I'll see you in the next course.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: Welcome to React Performance Patterns. I'm glad you're here, because this is one of those topics where most people have heard the vocabulary, memo, useMemo, useCallback, but very few have actually watched it make a measurable difference. That's what we're going to do in this course. We are not going to sprinkle optimizations around and hope. We are going to take an app that is slow on purpose, measure exactly where the time goes, and fix it one change at a time, checking after every change that the number actually moved. If a fix doesn't move the number, we throw it away. Okay? That's the rule for the whole course: measure, change one thing, measure again.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: So what are we building? A trading dashboard. Imagine the screen a trader keeps open all day. There's a table of five thousand rows, one per ticker symbol, and every row shows a symbol, a last price, a percent change, and a volume. Prices tick live, so rows keep updating several times a second. On top there's a filter bar where you can search by symbol, filter by sector, and sort by any column. The reason I picked this is that it is genuinely hard on React. Lots of rows, lots of updates, lots of derived data. If your tricks survive this app, they'll survive most apps you'll ever write.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: Let me show you the starting point. I'll open the project, and here's the structure. In the src folder we have App.jsx, Dashboard.jsx, FilterBar.jsx, PriceTable.jsx, and PriceRow.jsx. There's also a file called useTicks.js, which is a custom hook that fakes a live price feed with a timer. It updates a few hundred random symbols every second and hands us fresh data. Dashboard.jsx owns the state: the list of rows, the current filter text, the sort key, and the selected symbol. I wrote this version badly, deliberately. State lives too high, everything is recomputed on every render, and nothing is memoized. So when I run it and type in the search box, watch what happens.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: I type a single letter into the filter, and the input stutters. There's a visible delay between the key press and the character appearing. That is the bug we're hunting, and it's a very real kind of bug. Nothing is throwing an error, nothing is broken functionally, the table is correct. It's just slow, and slow is a feature users feel before they can describe it. Now, you might already have guesses about why. Maybe it's the filtering, maybe it's five thousand rows rendering, maybe it's the timer. Hold on to those guesses, because one of the lessons of this course is that guessing about performance is usually wrong, and that's why chapter two is entirely about profiling.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: A Dashboard That Lags on Purpose
text: Here's the road map. Chapter one is fundamentals: what React does when it renders, what actually triggers a re-render, and how React compares props. Chapter two is the React DevTools Profiler, where we find the wasted work. Chapter three is state placement and useMemo for computed data. Chapter four is React.memo and useCallback, plus the traps that quietly break them. Chapter five is rendering less, with virtualization and useTransition. And chapter six is where we profile the fixed dashboard and compare against today's numbers. You only need to be comfortable with components, props, state and hooks. Clone the starter project, run it, and type in that filter box so you feel the lag yourself. See you in the next lecture.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Before we optimize anything we need a precise picture of what React does when we say a component renders. This is where a lot of confusion starts, because the word render gets used for two completely different things. In this lecture I'll separate them: the render phase and the commit phase. Once you can hold those two in your head, a lot of performance advice suddenly makes sense, and a lot of folk wisdom turns out to be wrong. We'll use our dashboard as the example, so open Dashboard.jsx and PriceRow.jsx next to each other, because we'll keep jumping between them.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Start with the render phase. When React renders a component, all it does is call your function. That's it. Our PriceRow function runs, it reads its props, and it returns a description of what the UI should look like, which is a tree of plain objects we call React elements. Nothing has touched the browser yet. No DOM nodes were created, no text changed on screen. Rendering is just computing a description. That's why it's supposed to be pure: same props and state in, same description out. And notice that this means a render can be wasted. If PriceRow runs and returns exactly the description it returned last time, React did real work, your function body, for nothing.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Now the commit phase. After the render phase, React compares the new description with the previous one. This comparison is what people call reconciliation, or diffing. React walks the two trees, figures out the smallest set of changes, and only then it commits: it actually updates the DOM, changes the text node, sets the attribute, and runs layout effects. So here's the key idea. A component can render without anything being committed. If PriceRow renders but its price is still 101.25, the diff finds no difference, and the DOM is left completely alone. The browser does zero work. But your JavaScript still ran, and with five thousand rows, that JavaScript adds up fast.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: Let me make this concrete in the code. In PriceRow.jsx I'll add a console log at the top of the function: `console.log('render', symbol)`. I'll also open the Elements panel in the browser and turn on paint flashing so I can see DOM updates. Now I type in the filter box. The console floods with render messages, thousands of them, but the paint flashing shows only a few rows actually repaint. That gap is the whole story. Lots of renders, very few commits. The renders are pure overhead, JavaScript running to confirm that nothing changed. Our goal for the rest of this course is to close that gap, so React only calls the components whose output could actually be different.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Render vs Commit: What React Actually Does
text: One more thing, and it's a common misunderstanding. A render does not mean the DOM was rebuilt. React is not throwing away your page on every state change, and you shouldn't be afraid of renders as such. Renders are usually cheap. The trouble is when they're expensive, or when there are far too many of them, like our five thousand rows. So the question to ask is never how do I avoid all renders, it's how do I avoid the renders that don't change anything. Keep the console log in PriceRow, we'll lean on it, and in the next lecture we'll look at the exact events that cause React to start a render in the first place.

Let's answer the question that sits underneath everything in this course: what makes React re-render a component? If you can't answer that precisely, you'll end up memoizing the wrong things. And there's a very short list of triggers. I'll go through them one at a time and prove each one in the dashboard, using the console log we left in PriceRow. Open Dashboard.jsx, because most of what we'll talk about happens there. I'm going to try to convince you of one sentence that you should memorize, and then we'll spend the lecture seeing why it's true.

The first trigger is state. When a component calls its setter, say `setFilter`, React schedules a re-render of that component. The second trigger is context: when a value provided by a context provider changes, every component that reads that context re-renders. The third is a parent re-render. And here's the sentence. When a component renders, React renders all of its children, recursively, whether or not their props changed. That's the default behavior. Props changing is not a trigger at all. It's a common myth that a child re-renders because its props changed. It re-renders because its parent rendered. Props only matter once we opt in to checking them, which we'll do with React.memo later.

Let's prove it. In Dashboard.jsx we have `const [filter, setFilter] = useState('')`, and we pass `filter` to the FilterBar and also use it to compute the visible rows. The PriceTable receives `rows` as a prop and maps over them to render a PriceRow for each. Now I'll type one character. `setFilter` runs, Dashboard re-renders, so PriceTable re-renders, so every single PriceRow re-renders, even the ones whose symbol and price are exactly the same as before. Look at the console. Five thousand log lines for a single keystroke. The rows didn't ask for any of that. Their parent simply rendered, and the default is to keep going down the tree.

A second example is the live feed. The useTicks hook calls `setPrices` every second with a few hundred updated symbols. That state lives in Dashboard too. So every tick re-renders Dashboard, then the table, then all five thousand rows, even though only a few hundred prices actually changed. Do you see the pattern? State sits high in the tree, which means any change to it re-renders everything beneath. That's not a React bug. It's the design. React assumes renders are cheap and correctness matters more. Our job is to give it hints, through where we put state and through memoization, so it can skip the pointless work.

A few myths to clear up before we move on. Changing a ref does not trigger a re-render. A variable you reassign inside a component does not trigger one either. And calling a setter with the same value you already have usually bails out, though React may still render that one component once more before it bails. So the short list is: state, context, and parent renders. That's it. In the next lecture we'll look at how React decides whether two values are the same, because that comparison, shallow equality, is the mechanism behind almost every optimization we'll use, and also behind most of the ways they fail.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: This lecture is about one small idea that causes a huge share of real-world React performance bugs: shallow equality. Whenever React needs to ask whether something changed, whether that's a state update, a dependency array, or a memoized component's props, it uses basically the same check. It compares values with `Object.is`. If you understand exactly what that comparison does and does not look at, you can predict when memoization will work and when it will silently do nothing. We'll do a few experiments in a scratch file, so create one called equality.js and follow along.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: Start with primitives. `Object.is(5, 5)` is true. `Object.is('AAPL', 'AAPL')` is true. Numbers, strings, booleans compare by value, so two separate 101.25s are equal. Now objects. I'll write `const a = { price: 101.25 }` and `const b = { price: 101.25 }`, then `Object.is(a, b)`. That prints false. Same contents, but they're two different objects living at two different places in memory. Equality for objects, arrays and functions means same reference, not same contents. `Object.is(a, a)` is true, of course. Keep this in your head, because everything in the next three chapters is a story about references.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: Now what does shallow mean? When React.memo compares props, it takes the old props object and the new props object, and for each key it runs `Object.is` on the old value and the new value. It only goes one level deep. It doesn't look inside an object prop to compare its fields. So if a PriceRow receives `price={101.25}` and `symbol='AAPL'`, both primitives, that's a cheap and reliable comparison. But if it receives `quote={{ price: 101.25 }}` and the parent builds that object literal during every render, the reference is new every time, the shallow check says changed, and the component re-renders even though nothing meaningful changed.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: Here's where it bites in the dashboard. In Dashboard.jsx I compute `const visibleRows = rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter))`. Every render, `filter` creates a brand-new array. The contents might be identical, but the reference is new. So any memoized component receiving visibleRows would see a changed prop every time. The same goes for `const onSelect = (symbol) => setSelected(symbol)`, a new function on every render. Functions are objects too. And dependency arrays work the same way: useEffect and useMemo compare each dependency with `Object.is`, so an object dependency created inline will re-run the effect every single render.

lecture_title: 1.4 - Shallow Equality: How React Compares Props and State
text: So here's the model to carry forward. React does cheap reference checks, not deep comparisons, because deep comparison of big data would itself be expensive. That means our job as developers is to keep references stable when the data hasn't changed: keep the same array, the same object, the same function. Two tools help: useMemo for values and useCallback for functions. We'll build both properly in chapters three and four. But first, in chapter two, we're going to stop theorizing and use the Profiler to see which components are actually rendering for nothing in our dashboard. Make sure you can explain why those two identical objects aren't equal.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Time to stop guessing and measure. In this lecture we'll use the React DevTools Profiler on our dashboard. If you don't have the React Developer Tools browser extension installed, add it now for Chrome or Firefox. After you install it, open the dashboard, open your browser DevTools, and you'll see two new tabs: Components and Profiler. We'll use Profiler. One important setup note: profile a development build for learning, since it gives you component names and warnings, but remember that production is faster, so treat absolute numbers as relative, and compare before against after on the same machine.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Here's the workflow. In the Profiler tab there's a round record button. Before you click it, click the gear icon and turn on the option to record why each component rendered. That setting is the most useful one in the whole tool. Now press record, perform exactly one action, and press stop. I'll type a single letter into the filter box, then stop. The discipline matters here: one interaction per recording, otherwise you can't tell which work belongs to which action. If you record for ten seconds of random clicking, you'll get a pile of data you can't interpret.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Now we have a commit chart at the top. Each bar is one commit, one time React actually committed changes to the DOM, and its height and color show how long it took. Our single keystroke produced a tall yellow bar, around ninety milliseconds on my machine. For a smooth interface you want work per interaction under about sixteen milliseconds, since that's one frame at sixty frames per second. Ninety is more than five frames, which is exactly why the input feels sticky. Write that number down. This is our baseline: ninety milliseconds for one keystroke in the filter. Everything we do from here has to push that number down, and we'll check it each time.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: Click on that bar and the flame graph below shows the component tree for that commit. Each rectangle is a component, wide means it took more time, and the color tells you whether it rendered. Gray components didn't render in this commit. Colored ones did. Hover over PriceRow and the tooltip tells us the render time and, because we turned on the setting, why it rendered. For almost every row it says the parent component rendered. That confirms what we reasoned in chapter one: the rows render only because Dashboard did. Nothing about the rows themselves changed. We now have evidence rather than a hunch.

lecture_title: 2.1 - Profiling the Dashboard with React DevTools
text: There's also a ranked view, which sorts components by how long they took, slowest first. That's useful when one expensive component hides among thousands of cheap ones. In our case the ranked chart shows a wall of PriceRow entries, each tiny, but five thousand of them. Death by a thousand cuts, literally five thousand. That's the shape of problem we have. In the next lecture we'll read the flame graph more carefully, learn to tell useful renders from wasted ones, and build a short list of suspects. Before you move on, record your own baseline for one keystroke and keep the number.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: In the last lecture we recorded a baseline. Now we'll learn to read the flame graph for wasted renders, because that's the skill that tells you what to fix and, just as important, what to leave alone. A wasted render is one where the component's function ran and produced the same output as before. The Profiler can't say that directly in one click, but it gives us strong clues. We'll walk through a recording of the dashboard while a price tick arrives, not a keystroke this time, so we can see how the live feed behaves differently from the filter.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: I record one price tick from useTicks and stop. In the flame graph, the top component is App, then Dashboard, then FilterBar and PriceTable. Look at FilterBar. It rendered, shown in color. Why? The tooltip says the parent component rendered. But nothing about the filter changed. The filter box didn't care about a price tick, yet it re-ran. That's a cheap component so it doesn't matter much, and this is the first lesson: not every wasted render deserves a fix. Use the ranked view to focus on cost. A wasted render that takes zero point one milliseconds is noise. Five thousand of them are not.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: Now PriceTable and its PriceRow children. A tick updates a few hundred symbols. So for those few hundred rows, a render is legitimate, their price changed. But look at the flame graph: all five thousand rows are colored. The other four thousand seven hundred rendered for nothing. The Profiler's why-did-this-render tooltip tells us the same thing for each of them: parent rendered, props unchanged. That's the pattern to look for: a long run of identical siblings, all colored, all blamed on the parent. In our dashboard that is the single biggest cost, and it's what memoization will eventually address.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: Let's look at a different kind of clue: components that render much more often than you'd expect. Use the commit chart to step through several commits with the arrow keys, and watch which components light up each time. I see Dashboard in every commit, that's expected, it owns the state. But PriceTable also computes the visible rows by filtering and sorting five thousand items, on every commit, even a tick that doesn't change the sort order of anything the user cares about. In the ranked view that shows up as a single fat bar rather than a thousand thin ones. Thin and many means memoize children. Fat and single means avoid recomputing.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Reading the Flame Graph for Wasted Renders
text: So after this lecture we have a suspect list with evidence. One, state in Dashboard is too high, so everything beneath re-renders on every tick and keystroke. Two, the filter and sort computation runs every render. Three, the five thousand PriceRow components render regardless of whether their data changed. Four, inline functions and objects passed down probably defeat any memoization we add, but we'll verify that when we get there. Notice that these map directly to the next chapters. Chapter three handles one and two, chapter four handles three and four. Make a note of your own suspect list, and let's start fixing, beginning with where state lives.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: Our first real fix is the one that costs the least and often delivers the most: put state where it's used. Before we reach for any memoization hook, we should ask whether the state is in the right place at all. Remember the rule from chapter one: when a component re-renders, all its children re-render. So state held high up makes a large subtree re-render. If we move the state down into a smaller component, only that small subtree re-renders when it changes. Let's open Dashboard.jsx and see where the filter state lives right now.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: Currently `const [filter, setFilter] = useState('')` lives in Dashboard, right next to rows and the selected symbol. The filter is used in two places: the FilterBar, which shows the text input, and the visible row computation. Every keystroke calls setFilter, which re-renders Dashboard, which re-renders the table and its five thousand rows. Now, in this case the filter is genuinely needed by both the input and the table, so we can't just push it down into FilterBar. But there's another piece of state in Dashboard that is not shared: `hoveredSymbol`, used only by a small tooltip. That one is a perfect candidate to move down.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: Let's do it. I'll create a new component called SymbolTooltip in its own file. I cut `const [hovered, setHovered] = useState(null)` out of Dashboard and paste it into SymbolTooltip, along with the mouse handlers that set it. Now when the user hovers, only SymbolTooltip re-renders. The five thousand rows are untouched, because they aren't children of SymbolTooltip. Let me record this in the Profiler: hover over a row. Before the change the commit was sixty milliseconds, and now it's under two. That is a thirty-fold improvement without a single useMemo, only by moving a line of code.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: The second technique is lifting content up, which sounds like the opposite but is the same idea. Suppose we have a component that holds some state and wraps expensive children. For example, a ResizablePanel with a `width` state that wraps our PriceTable. When the width changes, the panel re-renders, and so does the table, because the table is rendered inside the panel's function. But if instead Dashboard renders the table and passes it as `children` to the panel, the table element is created by Dashboard, not by the panel. When the panel's state changes, React sees the same children element reference and skips it.

lecture_title: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up
text: This works because of what we learned about references. The children prop is an element object created in the parent. When the panel re-renders because of its own state, that prop is the same reference as before, so React doesn't need to re-render it. So the rule of thumb: first try to move state down to the component that needs it, and when a stateful wrapper surrounds slow content, pass the content in as children. These cost nothing, they have no dependency arrays to maintain, and they can't go stale. Only after that do we reach for memoization, which is exactly what we'll do in the next lecture. Re-record the hover interaction and write down your new number.

We moved state down, and that fixed the hover. Now let's deal with suspect number two, the filter and sort computation. Open Dashboard.jsx again. Right now, in the body of the component, we have `const visibleRows = rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter)).sort(compareBy(sortKey))`. That runs top to bottom on every render of Dashboard, and Dashboard renders on every price tick, every keystroke, and every selection change. Filtering five thousand rows and then sorting what's left is real work. Let me show you how much, using a little `console.time` around it, before we change anything.

I wrap the line with `console.time('visible')` and `console.timeEnd('visible')`, and then I trigger a price tick. The console says visible took about eleven milliseconds. Not terrible alone, but it runs on every tick, even when the filter and sort key are exactly what they were a second ago. Same inputs, same output, computed again. That's the situation memoization exists for. So before I write any code, let me explain what memoization is, because the word sounds fancier than it is. It's remembering. And React gives us a hook for it.

Memoization is an optimization technique where you cache the result of an expensive computation and return the cached result when the same inputs occur again instead of recomputing. In React, useMemo lets you memoize the result of a computation and only recompute it when its dependencies change. This is particularly valuable for computed state that derives from props or other state values and would otherwise be recalculated on every render even when the inputs have not changed. So that's the idea in the abstract. Now let's apply it to visibleRows, and I want you to notice what the inputs are: the rows array, the filter string, and the sort key. If none of those three changed, we should reuse the previous result. Those three values are our dependencies.

Here's the code. I'll write `const visibleRows = useMemo(() => { return rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter)).sort(compareBy(sortKey)) }, [rows, filter, sortKey])`. The first argument is the function that does the computation, and the second is the dependency array. React runs the function on the first render and stores the result. On later renders it compares each dependency to the previous one with `Object.is`, the shallow check from chapter one, and if they're all the same it returns the stored result without calling the function. I'll save and tick again. The console now shows the visible computation only when rows actually changes, and hovering or selecting no longer triggers it at all.

useMemo and useCallback are both memoization hooks but they serve different purposes. useMemo memoizes a computed value while useCallback memoizes a function reference. You need useCallback when you pass callbacks to child components that are themselves wrapped in React.memo, because without memoizing the callback the child still re-renders since it receives a new function reference on every parent render. The combination of React.memo on the child component and useCallback on the parent's callback prop is the complete pattern for preventing unnecessary child renders. Notice that second half especially, because it connects to the reference equality we've been building up since chapter one. We'll spend the whole next chapter on exactly that pattern, so for now just remember that useMemo handles values and useCallback handles functions.

Memoization helps computed state because it prevents redundant work during renders. If you have a filtered and sorted list derived from a large array of items, and the filter or sort criteria have not changed, there is no reason to redo that work. Without useMemo the filter and sort run on every render even when unrelated state updates trigger a re-render. With useMemo the computation is skipped entirely if the dependencies have not changed. The main pitfall is over-memoizing: adding useMemo everywhere without profiling first adds overhead from the dependency comparison that can actually be slower than just recomputing. Let's make that concrete with our dashboard. I removed the console.time wrappers, and the visible rows computation is now skipped on every render where its inputs are unchanged. One caution before we move on. A new rows array arrives with every tick, so on a tick the memo still recomputes, because rows changed. That's correct behavior. Memoization only saves work when the inputs truly stayed the same, and in the next lecture we'll look at when it isn't worth it at all.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: Last lecture we added useMemo, and it's tempting now to wrap everything in it. Please don't. In this lecture I want to show you the cases where useMemo costs more than it saves, because knowing when not to use a tool is half of using it well. Every useMemo call has a price. React has to store the previous value and the dependency array, and on every render it has to compare each dependency. Plus, you've made your code harder to read, and every future reader has to check that dependency list. That price is small, but if the thing you're memoizing is cheaper than the price, you've made things slower. So let's measure instead of guessing.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: Let me add a small example to Dashboard.jsx. Suppose I compute `const totalVolume = rows.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.volume, 0)` to show in the header. It looks like work, five thousand additions. So I wrap it in useMemo with `[rows]` as the dependency. Now let's profile both versions. Without useMemo, the reduce takes about point three milliseconds. With useMemo, on a tick the dependency changed anyway, since rows is a new array every tick, so the reduce runs again, plus React did the dependency comparison and the bookkeeping. We've paid extra for a cache that never hits.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: That's the first trap: a memo whose dependencies change on nearly every render is pure overhead. A cache only helps when it hits. The second trap is memoizing something trivial. Concatenating two strings, doing a few additions, building a tiny object, those take microseconds, less than the comparison cost. A useful rule of thumb from the React docs is to measure with `console.time`, and if the calculation takes a millisecond or more, consider memoizing it. You can even simulate a slower device by throttling the CPU in browser DevTools, to see which calculations would hurt on a phone.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: The third trap is the one that bites in real codebases: stale or wrong dependencies. If I write `useMemo(() => rows.filter(r => r.symbol.includes(filter)), [rows])` and forget `filter`, the list stops updating when the user types, because React thinks nothing relevant changed. The ESLint rule `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` catches this, so make sure you have it turned on, and don't silence it with a comment. A memoization bug is worse than a performance problem, since it gives you wrong output. And that's the point: every useMemo adds a promise you must keep up, that the dependency list is correct.

lecture_title: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves
text: So here's my decision procedure. First, can I fix this by moving state down or restructuring? Do that. Second, is the computation measurably slow, say a millisecond or more, and do its inputs often stay the same? Then use useMemo. Otherwise, skip it. In our dashboard, visibleRows passes both tests, and totalVolume fails both, so I'll remove that useMemo. We've now handled suspects one and two. Next chapter we get to the big one: the five thousand rows re-rendering for nothing, and the tools for that are React.memo and useCallback. Re-profile your keystroke before moving on.

Now we reach the part of the dashboard that hurts the most: five thousand PriceRow components re-rendering when only a few hundred prices changed. This is exactly what React.memo is for. Welcome to chapter four. In the Profiler we saw every row colored, blamed on the parent, with identical props. React.memo lets a component say, if my props are the same as last time, don't call me. So let's open PriceRow.jsx, where we have a plain function component that takes `symbol`, `price`, `change`, `volume`, and an `onSelect` callback, and see what happens when we wrap it.

By default a React component re-renders whenever its parent re-renders, even if its props did not change. React.memo wraps a component and skips the re-render when its props are shallowly equal to the previous render. The catch is shallow equality: primitives compare by value, but objects, arrays, and functions compare by reference. If a parent creates a new function or object literal on every render and passes it as a prop, React.memo sees a brand-new reference each time and re-renders anyway, defeating the optimization. Let's see that in our own code. I'll change the export in PriceRow.jsx to `export default React.memo(PriceRow)`. That's the entire change. Now save, record a single price tick in the Profiler, and look at the flame graph.

I expected the gray wall of skipped rows, and it's not there. Most rows are still colored, and the tooltip now says that the props changed, specifically `onSelect`. This is the reference trap we've been warning about since chapter one. In PriceTable.jsx, I map over the rows and write `<PriceRow key={r.symbol} {...r} onSelect={(s) => setSelected(s)} />`. That arrow function is created fresh on every render of the table. Same behavior, but a new function object each time, so the shallow comparison inside React.memo sees a changed prop for every single row and re-renders all of them. We added memo and got no benefit.

useCallback and useMemo exist to keep references stable across renders. useCallback returns the same function instance as long as its dependency array does not change, and useMemo does the same for a computed value. Wrapping a callback in useCallback before passing it to a React.memo child means the child actually sees a stable prop and can skip re-rendering. The rule of thumb: memoizing is only worth it when the child is expensive to render or the reference is consumed by a memoized child — wrapping everything adds overhead and dependency bugs for no benefit. So let's do exactly that. In Dashboard.jsx I'll write `const handleSelect = useCallback((symbol) => { setSelected(symbol) }, [])`. The dependency array is empty, because `setSelected` from useState is guaranteed to be stable, and we only use the symbol argument. Then I pass `onSelect={handleSelect}` down through PriceTable to each row. Now handleSelect is the same function instance on every render of Dashboard.

Save, record a tick, and look. Now the flame graph is mostly gray. Only the rows whose price actually changed are colored, a few hundred instead of five thousand. The commit that took ninety milliseconds drops to about eighteen. That's our first big, measured win in the main interaction. Check the keystroke too: typing in the filter now re-renders only the rows that enter or leave the visible list. Two things to remember. React.memo does nothing alone if the props contain fresh references. And useCallback does nothing alone if the child isn't memoized. They work as a pair, and next lecture we'll hunt the other ways to break that pair.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: We got memo working on PriceRow, but I want to be honest that it was fragile. One careless line anywhere in the chain and the entire optimization silently turns off, and nothing warns you. React will not tell you that memo is being defeated. So in this lecture we'll go looking for the most common culprits: inline objects, inline arrays, and inline functions passed as props. We'll deliberately break our own fix, watch the Profiler catch it, and then learn the habits that prevent it. Open PriceTable.jsx and PriceRow.jsx side by side.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: Let me add a feature that seems innocent. Each row needs a little style tweak depending on whether it's selected, so in PriceTable I write `<PriceRow key={r.symbol} {...r} style={{ color: r.change > 0 ? 'green' : 'red' }} onSelect={handleSelect} />`. Looks harmless, right? But the double curly braces mean an object literal, created fresh during every render of the table. New object, new reference, so shallow equality fails and memo re-renders every row again. I'll record a tick in the Profiler to confirm, and yes, the wall of colored rows is back, with the tooltip pointing to the style prop.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: There are a few ways out. The best one is not to pass an object at all. Pass primitives. Instead of a style object, pass `change={r.change}` and let PriceRow compute the color itself inside, since it already receives change as a number. Primitives compare by value, so memo works naturally. The second option is to hoist constants. If the object never changes, define it outside the component, like `const GREEN = { color: 'green' }`, so it's created once at module load and the reference is stable forever. The third option is useMemo for objects that really depend on props or state.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: The same applies to arrays and to functions that need arguments. Suppose each row has a remove button and we write `onRemove={() => removeSymbol(r.symbol)}`. That closure is new for each row on each render. A tidy fix is to pass the stable function and the symbol separately: `onRemove={removeSymbol}` along with the symbol, which the row already has, and then inside PriceRow the click handler calls `onRemove(symbol)`. Now the prop is the same function every time, and the child supplies its own argument. That pattern, stable callback plus data the child already knows, removes the need for per-row closures.

lecture_title: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo
text: Another subtle trap is the children prop. If you pass JSX as children to a memoized component, like `hi`, that JSX creates a new element object every render, so a memoized Card will re-render anyway. Same story: new reference. And the debugging approach is always the same. Record in the Profiler with the why-rendered setting on, look at which prop the tooltip blames, and find where that prop is created. A tip: React DevTools highlights memoized components with a Memo badge, which helps you confirm memo is actually applied. Next lecture, the most sneaky trap of all, context.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: There's one more way to defeat memoization, and it's the sneakiest, because React.memo cannot stop it at all: context. In this lecture we'll look at a re-render storm caused by context, and then fix it by splitting the context into pieces. Here's the setup. Our dashboard has a DashboardContext provided in App.jsx. It holds the selected symbol, the current filter, the user's watchlist, and the theme. Components deep in the tree, including PriceRow, read from it with `useContext(DashboardContext)`, because passing these through props felt tedious. And now we'll see the cost.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: The key fact: when a context value changes, every component that calls useContext for that context re-renders, regardless of React.memo. Memo only guards against re-renders caused by a parent. A context update goes straight to the consumers. In PriceRow I read `const { theme, selected } = useContext(DashboardContext)`. Now someone types in the filter, the provider value changes, and since all five thousand rows consume the context, all five thousand re-render, memo or not. I'll record the keystroke and confirm: the tooltip says context changed, and our memo wall is gone again.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: Why did the value change? In App.jsx the provider says `<DashboardContext.Provider value={{ selected, filter, watchlist, theme }}>`. That object literal is created on every render of App, so even a change to something unrelated produces a new object. And any change to any field, say filter, means every consumer sees a new value, even consumers that only use theme. Context has no selector. A consumer can't say that it only cares about one field. If you read the context, you re-render when any part of its value changes.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: The fix is to split the context by how often things change and who needs them. I'll make a ThemeContext holding only `theme`, a SelectionContext for `selected`, and a FilterContext for `filter`. The rows only need theme and selection, so they subscribe to those two and never see filter changes. The filter context is consumed only by FilterBar and the table. I also memoize each provider value with useMemo, so the value only changes when its actual contents change, for example `useMemo(() => ({ selected, setSelected }), [selected])`. Now typing in the filter no longer touches the rows.

lecture_title: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms
text: Another approach is to separate state from the functions that update it. Setters are stable, so put them in their own context, like SelectionDispatchContext, and components that only trigger changes will never re-render when the state changes. Let's check the result. Record the keystroke again and compare: the five thousand re-renders are down to the rows entering or leaving the filtered list. Quick summary of the rule. Keep context values small and focused, memoize provider values, and split by update frequency. If you need fine-grained subscription to a big store, look at libraries with selectors, but for most dashboards, splitting contexts is enough. Next up, rendering less.

We've cut the wasted renders, but there's still a fundamental problem we haven't touched: we're rendering five thousand rows into the DOM, when the screen shows about twenty. No amount of memoization changes that the browser must create and lay out five thousand table rows, and that has a real cost on first load and on every filter change. The fix is virtualization, sometimes called windowing: render only the rows that are visible, plus a small buffer, and fake the rest. Let's implement it in PriceTable.jsx. Open the Profiler first to see the commit time when the filter clears and all five thousand rows mount.

The baseline: clearing the filter takes about three hundred milliseconds, mostly mounting thousands of DOM nodes. Memo can't help here, since these are new mounts, not re-renders. Here's the idea. The table container has a fixed height, say six hundred pixels, and `overflow: auto`. Each row is a fixed height, say thirty-two pixels. So the total scrollable height is five thousand times thirty-two, one hundred sixty thousand pixels. We render one tall empty div with that height, so the scrollbar behaves as if all rows existed. Then we render only the rows whose position falls inside the visible window, absolutely positioned at the correct offset.

Let me write the core math. We track `scrollTop` in state, updated from the container's onScroll handler. The first visible index is `Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT)`. The number of visible rows is `Math.ceil(containerHeight / ROW_HEIGHT)`. We add an overscan, a few extra rows above and below, say five, so scrolling fast doesn't show blank gaps. Then `const visible = rows.slice(start, end)`. For each one, I render a PriceRow with `style={{ position: 'absolute', top: index * ROW_HEIGHT }}`. Note that the style object here is inline again, so I'll compute the offset inside the row from an `index` prop instead, to keep memo working.

In practice you'd probably use a library like react-window or TanStack Virtual, which handle edge cases such as variable heights, resize observers, and keyboard accessibility. I'm writing the core by hand so you understand what these libraries do, but for production, use the library. With react-window it looks like a `FixedSizeList` with `height`, `itemCount`, `itemSize`, and a row component that receives an `index` and a `style` prop. One more point: the library gives you a style object per row, and that's fine because it caches them, so memo still works when you wrap your row in React.memo.

Now the measurements. After virtualization, the DOM contains about thirty rows instead of five thousand. Clearing the filter takes under ten milliseconds. Scrolling stays smooth because we mount and unmount only a handful of rows per frame. A price tick re-renders only the visible rows whose prices changed, maybe three or four. There are trade-offs, though. Browser find-in-page can't see rows that aren't in the DOM, and screen reader users lose some context, so add aria attributes like the total row count. Virtualization is powerful but not free, which is why we did it after the cheap fixes. Next: keeping typing responsive with useTransition.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: Our table is cheap to render now, but there's one more problem I want to address, and it's about priority. When the user types in the filter, two things happen: the input's text must update right away, and the table must update to show the matching rows. If the table update is expensive, it can block the input from updating, and the typing feels laggy. But the input matters more than the table, and the table could wait a few milliseconds. React 18 gives us tools to say so. They're useTransition and useDeferredValue, and we'll use both in the dashboard.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: Start with useTransition. I'll open Dashboard.jsx and import it. `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()`. Currently the input's onChange does `setFilter(e.target.value)`, and that single state drives both the input value and the heavy table. I'll split it into two pieces of state. `inputValue` is the urgent one, bound directly to the input. `filter` is the one that drives the table. In the handler I write `setInputValue(value)` right away, then `startTransition(() => { setFilter(value) })`. The first update is urgent and renders immediately. The second is marked as a transition, a low-priority update.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: What does React do with a transition? It renders the transition update in the background, and if a more urgent update arrives, say the next keystroke, React interrupts the in-progress render, throws it away, and handles the urgent one first. This is why the input stays responsive even when the table rendering is slow. It's concurrent rendering. Also, `isPending` is true while the transition is in progress, so I can dim the table slightly, `opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1`, to show the user that results are catching up. The keystroke itself now commits in about two milliseconds, even when the table update lags behind.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: Now useDeferredValue, which is the same idea from the other direction. Sometimes you don't own the code that sets the state, for example the value comes from a prop. Then you can write `const deferredFilter = useDeferredValue(filter)` and use `deferredFilter` to compute the visible rows. React first renders with the old deferred value, so the urgent update finishes fast, then re-renders in the background with the new one. I'd use useTransition when I control the setter, and useDeferredValue when I only receive a value. For the dashboard, either works, and I'll keep the transition, since it also gives us isPending.

lecture_title: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering
text: One important caveat. These tools don't make the work faster, they make the app feel faster by prioritizing. The total render work is the same, or even slightly more if renders are interrupted and restarted. That's why we did the real optimizations first, and why we use transitions last, for the work that is still genuinely slow. Also, transitions only wrap state updates, not timers or fetches, and updates inside a transition can't be used to control a text input directly, which is why we kept inputValue separate. Next chapter, we'll measure everything together and compare against our baseline.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: It's time to close the loop. We started this course with a dashboard that took ninety milliseconds to handle a single keystroke, and we promised to measure every change. In this lecture we profile the fixed dashboard, and compare it against that baseline. Let's open the app, open the React DevTools Profiler, turn on record-why-rendered, and repeat exactly the same interaction we recorded in lecture two: type one letter into the filter box. Same machine, same browser, same data, same development build. If you change the conditions, the comparison means nothing, so be strict about that.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: I stop the recording and look at the commit chart. The bar that was ninety milliseconds yellow is now a short blue bar, around four milliseconds. In the flame graph, the FilterBar rendered, the table rendered with a handful of visible rows, and almost everything else is gray. The tooltip for the visible rows says the props changed, because those rows are legitimately showing different data. That's what a healthy profile looks like: components render when there's a reason and stay gray when there isn't.
