We went from ninety to four, over twenty times faster, and no single trick got us there.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: Let me list what contributed. Moving the hover state into SymbolTooltip cut that interaction from sixty milliseconds to two. useMemo on the visible rows skipped the filter and sort when inputs hadn't changed. React.memo on PriceRow plus useCallback for handleSelect took a tick from ninety to eighteen. Fixing the inline style object and splitting the context kept memo working. Virtualization cut mounting from five thousand rows to about thirty. And useTransition kept typing responsive. It's worth running a little experiment: turn each fix off one at a time and see which number moves. That tells you which fix pays the rent.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: Now let's try the stress test, the one that matters. I'll throttle the CPU to six times slower in the browser's Performance panel, which approximates a mid-range phone, and type quickly. The input stays responsive and the table catches up a moment later, dimmed while pending. On the original version the page froze for over half a second per keystroke under the same throttling. This is also a good habit for you: always check performance on a slow profile, not only on your fast laptop, because users don't all have your hardware.

lecture_title: 6.1 - Before and After: Profiling the Fixed Dashboard
text: A few honest caveats. First, development mode in React is slower than production, so run a production build and profile that too, using the Profiler build if you want numbers. Second, I'd keep a performance budget, a number like sixteen milliseconds per interaction, and re-check it when the codebase grows, because optimizations rot. Third, don't forget that these fixes added complexity: dependency arrays, memo boundaries, split contexts. Each one is a maintenance cost. So write down why each exists, ideally in a comment pointing to the measurement. In the final lecture, let's talk about where you can go from here.

Congratulations, you made it to the end of React Performance Patterns. Let's take a few minutes to step back, summarize what we did, and talk about where to go from here. We started with a trading dashboard that was deliberately slow, a five thousand row price table that stuttered on every keystroke and every live tick. We profiled it with the React DevTools Profiler, found the wasted work, and fixed it one measured change at a time. Along the way you learned the concepts underneath the fixes, and I think those matter more than the specific code.

Let me restate the mental model in a few sentences. A render is calling your function, and a commit is touching the DOM. Components re-render because of state, context, or because their parent rendered, never simply because props changed. React compares props and dependencies with shallow reference checks, which means that keeping references stable is the central skill. Moving state down and lifting content up are free fixes. useMemo caches expensive derived values. React.memo and useCallback work as a pair. Inline objects, functions and context values quietly break them. And virtualization and transitions handle what's left.

The workflow matters more than any single hook. Measure first with a baseline, form a hypothesis from the Profiler, change one thing, and measure again. If a change doesn't move the number, remove it. This protects you from the most common failure in performance work, which is cluttering a codebase with optimizations that do nothing and make future changes harder. Remember our totalVolume example, where useMemo made things slightly worse. Evidence beats intuition, including mine, so try the techniques from this course on your own projects and see which ones actually show up in your profiles.

Here's what I'd suggest as next steps. First, take the dashboard and extend it: add a second table with sparklines, or a column that does a heavier computation, and profile what breaks. Second, read about React Compiler, which aims to apply memoization automatically at build time; understanding the manual patterns in this course will help you know what it does for you and where it can't. Third, explore tools such as why-did-you-render, the React Profiler API for measuring in production, and Web Vitals like Interaction to Next Paint, which measures the exact thing we tuned: input responsiveness.

Finally, a challenge. Pick a real component in a project you work on, one you suspect is slow, and write down its current number from the Profiler before changing anything. Then apply exactly one technique from this course and measure again. Share the before and after with someone, because explaining a measured improvement is the best way to cement it. Thank you for sticking with it, for typing in that laggy filter box more times than any reasonable person should, and for building the habit of measuring first. Go make something fast, on purpose. I'll see you in the next course.
